# ADR-0010: Self-describing tool descriptions instead of a `SKILL.md` file

## Status

Accepted (simplify-skill-tool-delivery, 2026-09). Partly superseded by
[ADR-0020](0020-steer-agent-to-context-tools.md): descriptions remain the
main channel, but a system-prompt hint and a bundled `index-status` skill
were added.

## Context

OpenCode has a `skill` mechanism: a plugin can ship a `SKILL.md` file
that the agent discovers and loads via a `skill({name})` call before
using the capability it describes. An earlier iteration of this
plugin's design considered delivering workflow guidance (e.g. "prefer
`grep`/`glob` for exact identifier lookups; use `semantic_search` for
conceptual/fuzzy queries instead") via a `SKILL.md`.

OpenCode already surfaces every registered tool's `description` field
to the agent at tool-listing time, alongside every built-in tool
(`grep`, `glob`, `lsp`, etc.) -- the agent sees it "for free" as part of
normal tool discovery, before ever deciding whether to call anything.

## Decision

Carry the workflow guidance directly in each tool's `description`
string (e.g. `semantic_search`'s description explicitly says when to
prefer `grep`/`glob` instead), rather than via a separate `SKILL.md`
file and its associated discovery mechanism.

## Consequences

- No extra discovery round trip: a `SKILL.md`-based approach requires
  the agent to have already decided the skill is relevant enough to
  invoke `skill({name})` before it can read the guidance that would
  have helped it decide that in the first place. Description-embedded
  guidance is visible up front, at the same time every other tool's
  description is.
- Less indirection for maintainers too: the guidance lives right next
  to the tool definition it applies to (`src/tools/semantic-search.ts`
  etc.), not in a separate file that has to be kept in sync with the
  tool's actual behavior.
- This only applies to per-tool workflow guidance. It does not rule out
  a `SKILL.md`/skill mechanism for something that genuinely needs
  cross-tool, multi-step workflow orchestration guidance beyond what a
  single tool's description can carry -- this plugin simply hasn't
  needed that yet.

## Alternatives considered

- **A `SKILL.md` describing when/how to use `semantic_search` vs.
  native tools.** Rejected for the reason above: strictly adds
  indirection for a single-tool workflow hint that fits naturally in
  the tool's own description field.

# ai-context plugin: codebase context workflow

The tools are native opencode tools provided by this plugin (no MCP server,
no Docker). Prefer them over grep/glob for conceptual questions. Details:
`docs/tools.md`.

1. `repo_structure` — first, for orientation: directories with file counts and
   languages. Narrow with `dir_path` and `depth`.
2. `semantic_search(query)` — conceptual questions about **source code**
   ("where do we retry failed requests?"). Hybrid vector + FTS5 ranking with
   re-ranking; hits include path, line range and symbol. Chunks of type
   `file-summary` describe a whole file (LLM-written when `summary_llm` is
   reachable, deterministic otherwise). Follow up with `read` on the line range.
3. `find_symbol(query, [kind])` — you know part of a class/function/method
   name. Returns definitions plus likely covering tests. For exact references
   use opencode's native `lsp` tool (1.x) or `analyze_impact` (2.x).
4. `analyze_impact(symbolName, [path], [direction], [depth])` — before
   changing, renaming or removing a symbol: callers, callees, importers and
   covering test files. Edges are name-based; ambiguous ones are flagged, so
   confirm with `lsp` (1.x) or by reading the call site (2.x).
5. `search_docs(query, [mode])` — Markdown docs, ADRs, RFCs. Documents are
   stored as heading trees (PageIndex style), never as code chunks. Modes:
   `toc_only` → `summary_only` (default) → `node_text`, drilling down.
6. `index_status` — when results are empty/partial or carry an
   `indexingNotice`; shows progress and failed files.

Other indexed repos: use the `cross-repo` skill (`ai_context_list_projects`,
`ai_context_allow_repo`, then the `project` argument).

Stop as soon as you have enough context; don't call every tool by default. If
`semantic_search` finds nothing after one rephrase, say so instead of guessing.

# IntelliJ IDEA MCP - Router

This is the entry point for all work done through the IntelliJ IDEA MCP server. It does not contain the detailed tool
guidance itself - it routes to a bundled reference file for the job at hand. Read the matching reference below before
calling any IDE MCP tool (note: despite the `idea_*` naming used loosely below and by users referring to "IDEA MCP
tools" generically, this session's live tool schema exposes bare names with **no `idea_` prefix** — e.g. `read_file`,
not `idea_read_file`; confirmed live 2026-08-13, see `references/tool-routing-contract.md` for the corrected table).

**Read `references/tool-routing-contract.md` FIRST, before any other reference in this skill.** It is the binding,
single-page decision table for which tool to use per action (including the git-commit exception); the other reference
files below give supporting detail, but the contract is what's actually enforced (via the session's `tool_ledger`
table - see that file for how compliance is logged and queried, not just stated).

## Core principle

IDEA MCP tools operate on the **live IDE index** (semantic, not text-based). Prefer them over shell/grep/cat whenever
the project is open in the IDE. Use them for precise, targeted operations once you know (or can find) the file/symbol in
question.

## Pick the right guidance

| Task                                                                                                                                                    | Read                           |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Find/understand code: symbol lookup, usages, file structure, project dependencies/modules, compile errors/warnings                                      | **`references/explore.md`**    |
| Change code: create/edit files, apply text edits, reformat, rename/extract/move/change-signature refactorings                                           | **`references/edit.md`**       |
| Build the project, run configurations or tests, use the IDE terminal, VCS status/diff, run notebooks, generate/run custom inspections                   | **`references/ops.md`**        |
| Working inside an IntelliJ **plugin** project or the JetBrains **platform monorepo** itself (extension points, plugin.xml, threading/lock requirements) | **`references/plugin-dev.md`** |
| Need **runtime** evidence: breakpoints, stepping, stack/frame values, expression evaluation, confirming whether code is reached                         | **`references/debugger.md`**   |

Read only the reference (s) needed for the current step - don't read all of them upfront. A single task often chains
several: e.g. read `references/explore.md` to locate the bug -> read `references/debugger.md` to confirm root cause ->
read `references/edit.md` to fix it -> read `references/ops.md` to build/test.

## Workflow

1. Classify the request using the table above.
2. Read the matching file under `references/` in this skill before calling any tool it covers.
3. Each reference file opens with its own **Activation Gate**: a check of which tools must actually be available in the
   current MCP session (and, for `references/plugin-dev.md`, whether the project even applies) before that guidance
   should be used. Respect it - if a gate fails, state the blocker explicitly instead of silently falling back to a
   different toolset or guessing tool names.
4. If the task spans multiple phases (explore -> debug -> fix -> verify), read each piece of guidance in turn as you
   reach that phase, in the order the work actually proceeds.
5. Never fall back to shell/file tools for something an IDE MCP tool already covers - the IDE-native tool understands
   language semantics (imports, references, code style) that text tools don't.
6. Always pass `projectPath` when known, to avoid ambiguous resolution across multiple open projects.

## When NOT to use this router

- Open-ended "what does this module/service do?" questions with no specific target - prefer whatever semantic/context
  search tools are available for broad exploration, and only switch to IDEA MCP once you have a concrete file/symbol
  target.

# Build and install ai-context-opencode-plugin

Run from `ai-context-opencode-plugin/`. Stop at the first failing step and fix
it before continuing. Commits are made by the user.

2. `npm run test:unit` (a plugin test can flake once; rerun before debugging)

4. `./scripts/install-plugin.sh` (installs the bundle and worker, ensures runtime deps)
5. Verify: `ls -l dist/accso-ai-context.js ~/.config/opencode/plugins/accso-ai-context.js` shows a fresh timestamp.

# Cross-repo lookup

Every repo is isolated by default: `semantic_search` only sees its own index.
The other repo must already be indexed (opened once with this plugin).

## 1. Find the exact project name

Call `ai_context_list_projects` BEFORE assuming a library or repo is not
indexed. Each entry has a `name` (e.g. `tlt-platform`) and a `key`
(`<name>-<hash8>`). Use only the `name`: the hash differs per machine.
Never guess a name; pick the one matching what the user named.

## 2. Allow it (once, persistent)

Call `ai_context_allow_repo` with that name. It is validated against the
registry and stored (as name, shareable with the team) in `allowed_repos` in `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml`. It
takes effect immediately, no restart. Only do this when the user asked for
the other repo's results.

## 3. Query it

- `semantic_search`: results of allowed repos are merged in, each tagged with
  its `project`.
- `repo_structure`, `find_symbol`, `analyze_impact` and `search_docs`: pass
  `project: "<name>"` to look into that repo instead of the current one.
- Paths in results are relative to THAT repo, not to the current worktree.
  To read the files, ask the user for the repo's location; `read` only
  works inside the current project.

## Troubleshooting

- `Unknown or not allowed project`: run step 1 and 2. A hashed key is not accepted.
- Name missing in the list: that repo was never indexed with this plugin.
- No symbols or docs from that repo: its symbol index or doc trees may not exist yet.

# Index status — follow and tune plugin indexing

The plugin writes `.opencode/ai-context/index-status.json` in the project
worktree (atomically, at most every 2 s). It is the only progress channel that
works under ACP; OS popups only mark start/finish/failure.

## 1. Read it once

```bash
cat .opencode/ai-context/index-status.json
```

Fields: `phase` (`idle|scanning|loading-model|indexing|done|failed`), `done`,
`total`, `percent`, `etaSeconds`, `filesPerSec`, `currentFile`, `failed`,
`failures[]` (file, error, attempts), `lastError`.

## 2. Live view: give the user the command

When the user wants to follow progress live, do this and nothing more:

1. Read the JSON file once (step 1) and report phase, percent, ETA and
   failures in a few lines.
2. Give the user this command to run in their own terminal (replace
   `<worktree>` with the absolute project path):

```bash
<worktree>/.opencode/skills/index-status/scripts/watch-index-status.sh
```

NEVER run `watch-index-status.sh` yourself, with any tool: it loops forever,
blocks or aborts your call, and the user cannot see its output. macOS has no
`watch`; the script (uses `jq` if present, plain `cat` otherwise) is the
replacement. Do not start loops or background watchers either.

## 3. Interpret

- `loading-model`: first embedding call downloads/loads the model; normal, one time.
- `failed` + `lastError` mentioning `max_memory_mb`: the memory guard stopped
  indexing. Lower `embed_max_tokens`/`max_file_bytes` or raise `max_memory_mb`.
- `failures[]` with `skipped: file is N bytes`: file over `max_file_bytes`; it is
  skipped and retried automatically when it changes.
- Fan/CPU high: lower `embed_threads` (default 2).
- Noise from generated/legacy code: add patterns to `exclude:`.

All keys live in `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml` (auto-created, commented).
Restart opencode after editing it.

# ai-context-opencode-plugin

A native [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) plugin that gives the agent a local,
Docker-free code index (indexing and search run locally; see the data boundary below): semantic search, repository structure, call/import
impact analysis and document search. It replaces the Docker-based MCP server,
LSP bridge and file watcher of this repo's `.ai-context/` stack.

Each multi-chunk file also gets an L1 summary chunk, written by a local
OpenAI-compatible LLM (LM Studio, Ollama, oMLX; configure `summary_llm`) and
falling back to a deterministic summary when none is reachable (rewritten
automatically once the LLM answers; `reindex_summaries` forces it). Search combines
vectors with FTS5 BM25 and a small cross-encoder re-ranker; other indexed repos
can be searched via an allowlist.

Works in the opencode TUI and under ACP (JetBrains AI Assistant). The embedding
model runs in one shared background process, so the opencode host stays small.

> **Data boundary:** indexing, embeddings and search run locally, but the
> plugin cannot control what the agent does with the results. Retrieved code
> and documents become part of the conversation and go to your configured model
> provider, which may not be local. See [docs/data-boundary.md](docs/data-boundary.md).

## Tools

| Tool | For |
| --- | --- |
| `repo_structure` | Directory layout, file counts, languages |
| `semantic_search` | Conceptual questions about source code |
| `find_symbol` | Where a class/function/method is defined, by name |
| `analyze_impact` | Callers/callees/importers before changing a symbol |
| `search_docs` | Markdown docs, ADRs, RFCs |
| `index_status` | Indexing progress and index health |
| `ai_context_*` | Admin: projects, backup, index tree, allowlist, rescan, telemetry |

On OpenCode 2.x the first six are direct tools and the `ai_context_*` tools are reached through Code Mode (`execute`). Details: [docs/tools.md](docs/tools.md).

## Quickstart

```bash
npm install
npm run build
./scripts/install-plugin.sh
```

Restart opencode. The plugin is opt-in per repository: the generated
`.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml` has `enabled: false`; set it to `true` and
restart. The first index takes minutes; follow it in
`.opencode/ai-context/index-status.json`. Next to it: `index-tree.md` (which files are indexed, with date/repo/branch) and `error.log.md` (what failed and why). More: [docs/installation.md](docs/installation.md).

**OpenCode versions.** The bundle serves OpenCode 2.x (`setup(ctx)`, `@opencode/plugin`) and
1.x (`server()`, >= 1.18.29) from one default export ([ADR-0031](docs/adr/0031-opencode-2x-entry-and-search-steering.md)).
**LSP:** on 1.x the plugin enables the built-in LSP servers (unless `lsp: false`) and points the
agent to the native `lsp` tool; opencode only registers that tool when
`OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL=true` is set in the environment that starts opencode (setting it
from inside the plugin may come too late). OpenCode 2.x runs no language servers, so there the
plugin works from the index alone (`find_symbol`, `analyze_impact`) and never mentions `lsp`.
A plugin-owned LSP bridge for both is planned: [docs/lsp-roadmap.md](docs/lsp-roadmap.md).

Indexing follows file changes through opencode's file watcher on 1.x (opt-in via
`OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_FILEWATCHER`, which the plugin sets itself, best effort). OpenCode 2.2
has no project-wide watcher event for plugins (`filesystem.changed` only fires for files
watched through its experimental `fs.watch` API), so on 2.x (and whenever the 1.x watcher is
silent) the index is kept fresh from tool calls: `edit`/`write`/`apply_patch` index just the touched files, `shell`/`bash` and IDE tools trigger a full rescan shortly after, and a finished session (`session.idle`, at most every 30 s) rescans for changes made outside the agent, and `ai_context_rescan` does it on demand.
Fingerprints skip unchanged files, so a rescan is cheap.

**Steering away from grep/glob.** Agents tend to start with `glob **/*.kt` or a descriptive
`grep`. The plugin counters this in three places: a rule block in the system prompt, a
suffix on the native `grep`/`glob` tool descriptions, and a one-line note appended to the
result of a grep/glob call that looks exploratory (extension-only glob, multi-word or
many-branch pattern, empty result). All three follow `agent_hint` in the config file.

## Metrics export (opt-in)

# Architecture The plugin runs **inside the opencode host process** (Bun, also under ACP in the JetBrains AI Assistant). The memory-heavy embedding model runs in one **shared worker process** per user. Everything else is local files. ## Components ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Host["opencode host (one per session/ACP instance)"] Hooks["hook/plugin.ts
tools + event + system hook"] Idx["Indexer
chunk · graph · doc-tree"] Search["Search
vector · keyword · doc-tree · graph"] Obs["Observability
status file · OS notify · OTel"] end subgraph Worker["shared embedding worker (1 per user)"] ORT["onnxruntime-node
nomic-embed-text-v1.5"] end subgraph Store["~/.local/share/ai-context-opencode-plugin/projects/<key>"] V[("index.sqlite
chunks + vectors")] D[("doc trees")] G[("symbol/import/call graph")] end WT[".opencode/ai-context/
status · backup"] Hooks --> Idx --> V & D & G Hooks --> Search --> V & D & G Idx -- "embed (unix socket, NDJSON)" --> ORT Search -- "embedQuery" --> ORT Idx --> Obs --> WT Hooks -. backup .-> WT ``` ## Indexing pipeline ```mermaid flowchart TD A["startup reconciliation walk
or file.watcher.updated (debounced)"] --> B{"file filter
.gitignore · extensions · exclude · max_file_bytes"} B -- skip --> X["status file: skipped"] B -- ok --> C{"Markdown and tree-eligible?"} C -- yes --> T["doc-tree builder → doc-tree store"] C -- no --> D["chunker chain
tree-sitter → regex → data-format → paragraph"] D --> E["decorator fix · dispatch sub-chunking · token-budget split"] E --> F["embedDocument (worker)"] F --> G["vector store (delta upsert)"] B -- ok --> H["graph extractor → symbols, imports, calls"] G & T & H --> P["progress → status file, OS notices, memory guard"] ``` Delta indexing: unchanged files are skipped, removed or newly excluded files are purged. Failures are skipped with a note (file, error, attempts) instead of aborting the run. ## Query flow ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Ag as Agent participant Pl as Plugin tool participant W as Embedding worker participant S as SQLite stores Ag->>Pl: semantic_search(query) Pl->>W: embedQuery W-->>Pl: vector Pl->>S: vector + FTS5 BM25 search, own + allowlisted projects (live, no restart) S-->>Pl: candidates (fused per store by RRF) Pl->>W: cross-encoder rerank (if reranker enabled) Pl->>Pl: merge across projects, slice Pl-->>Ag: chunks + indexingNotice? Ag->>Ag: read file at line range ``` ## Process model ```mermaid flowchart LR I1["opencode acp #1"] & I2["opencode acp #2"] & I3["opencode acp #3"] -- socket --> W["embedding worker
~0.4-0.55 GB"] W -. "idle 10 min or RSS limit → exit" .-> E((exit)) I1 -. # Configuration

Precedence, highest first: explicit function option (tests only) > env var >
`.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml` (team-shared, committable) > built-in
default ([ADR-0014](adr/0014-project-config-file-precedence.md)). The file is
auto-created on first start with every key and its default value; restart
opencode after editing it. The generated file is the reference for every
setting (default, effect, environment variable); there is no separate example file. The plugin is **opt-in per repository**
([ADR-0029](adr/0029-opt-in-enabled-flag-and-default-template.md)): the
generated file has `enabled: false`, and while it is off (or the key is missing)
the plugin only keeps the file and does nothing else. Set `enabled: true` to
switch it on.

| `summary_llm` | - | oMLX `http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1`, `Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct-MLX-4bit` | Block `base_url`, `model` (exact name), `api_key_env?`, `timeout_ms?`; `false` disables the LLM. The API key is never read from the file (a literal `api_key` is ignored with a warning): export it as `AI_CONTEXT_SUMMARY_LLM_API_KEY` or the variable named by `api_key_env`; without one no key is sent. On HTTP 401 the user gets an OS popup and an `index_status` notice ("API key not set. Set it with: export AI_CONTEXT_SUMMARY_LLM_API_KEY=<your key> and restart opencode"). Failures fall back to deterministic summaries, which are flagged (`detsum` in the stored fingerprint) and rewritten, summary only, on a later start once the LLM answers; Markdown doc-tree summaries are skipped. Also writes the doc-tree node summaries. Requests carry `tool_choice: "none"` (retried without it on HTTP 400) so servers that inject global MCP tools answer with prose; answers that are JSON tool calls are rejected. File content is sent to `base_url`; keep it local ([data boundary](data-boundary.md)). |
| `reindex_chunks` / `reindex_summaries` | - | `false` | One-off, reset to `false` by the plugin after a finished run. `reindex_chunks` re-chunks and re-embeds every file (stored summaries kept), `reindex_summaries` rewrites the file summaries only, both `true` re-index everything. A failed or aborted run keeps the flags on. |
| `shared_worker` | `AI_CONTEXT_SHARED_WORKER=0` | `true` | Run embeddings in one shared background process. |

`AI_CONTEXT_PROJECT_FILES=0` disables writing project files (config, skill,
gitignore); used by the unit tests.

At startup the plugin sets `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_FILEWATCHER=true` (best effort) so OpenCode 1.x runs its file watcher, unless you set `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER` to anything other than `0`/`false`. OpenCode 2.x ignores the flag; see the README for how indexing stays fresh there.

# Data boundary: what is local, what is not

The plugin itself works locally. It does **not** control what happens to the
data after it has been handed to the agent.

## Stays on your machine (the plugin)

- Indexing, chunking, embeddings (ONNX, shared worker), re-ranking, SQLite
  stores and the call/import graph. No code or query is sent anywhere by the
  plugin's index and search path.
- File and document summaries use the `summary_llm` endpoint. The default is
  a local server (`127.0.0.1`). The plugin sends file content there. Its API
  key comes from an environment variable only, never from the committed config.
- The repo-local backup (`.opencode/ai-context/backup/`) is plain text that
  contains chunk text, doc trees and the symbol graph. It lives in the
  repository, so committing and pushing it publishes that content to whatever
  hosts the repo.

## Outside the plugin's control

- **Tool results go to the agent's LLM.** Everything `semantic_search`,
  `search_docs`, `find_symbol`, `analyze_impact`, `repo_structure` and the
  admin tools return (code snippets, document text, summaries, paths, status)
  becomes part of the conversation. opencode (or the ACP client) then sends it
  to the configured model provider. If that provider is a cloud service, the
  retrieved code leaves the machine, under that provider's terms and retention.
  The plugin cannot detect or restrict this.
- **Cross-repo search** (allowlist) makes other indexed projects' content
  retrievable, and therefore sendable, in the same way.
- **`summary_llm`**: pointing `base_url` at a remote endpoint sends file
  content to that endpoint.
- Hints and skills the plugin installs only steer the agent; they are not an
  access control.

## Recommendations

- For confidential code, use a model provider you consider local or
  contractually acceptable, not just a local index.
- Keep `summary_llm` on a local server.
- Review `allowed_repos` in `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml` before enabling cross-repo search.
- `tool_log_full_responses: true` writes tool responses (repo code) to the git-ignored `tool.log.md`; do not attach that file to bug reports unreviewed.
- Check the backup content before committing it to a shared or public repo.
- Exclude sensitive paths from indexing (`exclude`, see [configuration](configuration.md)).

## Workflow

Test first: write or update the failing test, implement, then run
`npm run typecheck` and `npm run test:unit`. Keep steps small; one decision
that is hard to reverse gets an ADR in [adr/](adr/README.md).

## Testing

- All tests are unit tests in `test/unit/` (`node:test`); stores use temporary
  directories, embedders and workers are injected fakes.
- `test:unit` sets `AI_CONTEXT_OS_NOTIFICATIONS=0`, `AI_CONTEXT_INSTALL_SKILLS=0`,
  `AI_CONTEXT_PROJECT_FILES=0` and `AI_CONTEXT_SHARED_WORKER=0` so tests never
  pop up notifications, write project files or spawn a worker.
- Mock stores must provide `listFiles`, `getChunksPage`, `getIndexStatus`
  (and `countTrees`, `listPaths` for doc-tree stores).
- `test/unit/tool-descriptions.test.ts` locks the tool naming scheme and the
  essential description content.
- Tests that open timers or sockets must close them; a leaked handle hangs the
  run (the worker's idle timer once did).

## Conventions

- Prefer the code intelligence of the IDE; no new dependency without need.
- Changing how files are chunked, tree-indexed or summarized? Bump `CODE_INDEX_VERSION` /

- Comments only where the code needs clarification.

# Installation

The plugin is one bundled file plus one worker script, installed into
opencode's **global** config directory so one install covers every repo
([ADR-0015](adr/0015-single-bundled-plugin-file.md)).

```bash
npm install
npm run build              # dist/accso-ai-context.js + dist/ai-context-worker.mjs
./scripts/install-plugin.sh
# or, on a fresh machine: mise install && mise run setup
#   (setup runs npm install, build and the installer; mise install provides Node 22)
```

Then restart opencode (all running instances). On OpenCode 2.x the plugin is reloaded automatically (or run `/reload`); 1.x needs a restart.

## What the installer does

| Target | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `~/.config/opencode/plugins/accso-ai-context.js` | the plugin bundle |
| `~/.config/opencode/ai-context-worker.mjs` | shared embedding worker (kept outside `plugins/` on purpose: opencode loads every file there as a plugin) |
| `~/.config/opencode/package.json` | merged native dependencies (`onnxruntime-node`, `tokenizers`, tree-sitter grammars, ...) |

It runs `bun install` there (npm as fallback) and verifies every package,
including each grammar's `.wasm`; it exits non-zero otherwise. Set
`SKIP_DEPS_INSTALL=1` to leave dependency installation to opencode's next
start. Re-running is safe: only this plugin's own entries are touched.

## First start

- The embedding model (~137 MB, quantized ONNX) is downloaded once into the
  shared Hugging Face cache ([ADR-0005](adr/0005-shared-huggingface-model-cache-directory.md)).
- `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml` is created if missing (every setting with
  its default, `enabled: false`, never overwritten). **The plugin does nothing
  in a repository until you set `enabled: true` there** (or start opencode with
  `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_ENABLED=1`). Once enabled, it also creates `.opencode/.gitignore` (volatile status file) and the
  `index-status` and `cross-repo` skills under `.opencode/skills/`. The `.opencode` folder is
  created if it does not exist.
- The first index of a repo can take minutes; follow it in
  `.opencode/ai-context/index-status.json` or via `index_status`.

## Updating

Rebuild, re-run `install-plugin.sh`, restart opencode (2.x: reloads on its own). The shared worker is
replaced automatically once the old one exits (idle 10 min) or you stop it.

## Uninstalling

Remove the two files above and, if wanted, the data directory
`~/.local/share/ai-context-opencode-plugin/`.

# LSP roadmap

## Where we are (2026-10-28)

OpenCode 2.x keeps the `lsp` config schema (`command`, `extensions`, `disabled`, `env`,
`initialization`) but does not run language servers, expose an LSP tool, an LSP API or
diagnostics. On 2.x the plugin therefore does not enable LSP and never points the agent at an
`lsp` tool. On OpenCode 1.x nothing changed: it still enables the built-in LSP and uses the
native `lsp` tool ([ADR-0031](adr/0031-opencode-2x-entry-and-search-steering.md)).

What replaces it today: `find_symbol` (definitions by name) and `analyze_impact` (callers,
callees, importers, tests) from the tree-sitter graph. The graph is name-based; ambiguous
edges are flagged and confirmed by reading the call site.

## Goal

Exact answers where the graph guesses: go to definition, find references, incoming/outgoing
calls, hover/type info, workspace symbols, plus diagnostics after edits. Delivered by the
plugin itself, since the host will not.

## Plan

1. **Spike (1-2 days).** One language end to end (Kotlin, the most used in the target repos;
   `kotlin-language-server` or JetBrains' server). A small stdio JSON-RPC client
   (`initialize`, `textDocument/definition|references|prepareCallHierarchy`, `workspace/symbol`)
   without a library or with `vscode-jsonrpc`. Measure start-up time and memory on a real repo.
2. **Server manager.** `src/lsp/`: lazy start on first use, one process per (language, project),
   idle timeout, memory cap shared with the existing memory guard, crash restart with backoff,
   clean shutdown in the plugin cleanup. Reuse the user's `lsp` config block from
   `opencode.json` (same schema, so a 1.x/2.x config keeps working) with built-in defaults
   for the languages in the graph.
3. **Tool surface.** One tool `code_navigate` (actions: `definition`, `references`,
   `incoming_calls`, `outgoing_calls`, `workspace_symbol`, `hover`) taking `path`, `line`,
   `character` or a symbol name resolved through `find_symbol` first. Results in the same JSON
   style as the other tools, capped and with file/line for `read`.
4. **Graph integration.** `analyze_impact` upgrades ambiguous edges through LSP when a server
   is up (`confirmed: true/false`), and falls back to the graph otherwise. The hint then offers
   `code_navigate` instead of reading call sites.
5. **Diagnostics (optional).** After `edit`/`write`, notify the server and append new errors
   to the tool result (like the nudge mechanism), so the agent sees compile errors without
   running the build.
6. **Steering.** Add one line to the agent hint and a suffix for the native `read`/`grep`
   descriptions only after step 3 ships and measurably helps (telemetry `adoption` view).

## Decisions needed before step 2

- Which languages first (Kotlin, TypeScript, Java, Python?) and who provides the server
  binaries (user-installed vs. downloaded to the shared model cache dir).
- Whether to reuse an LSP the IDE already runs (JetBrains MCP/`idea` tools) instead of
  spawning our own for IntelliJ users.
- Resource budget: language servers are heavy (Kotlin: 1+ GB); must respect `max_memory_mb`.

## Risks

- Start-up and indexing time of servers (minutes on large Gradle projects): the tool must
  report "server still indexing" like `indexingNotice` instead of blocking.
- Per-language setup quirks (build tool, SDK paths); keep it opt-in per language.
- Possible future native 2.x LSP support: keep the tool name and schema separate from the
  transport so we can switch to it if OpenCode ships one.

# Observability

This plugin exposes telemetry through two complementary channels, and
separately has to solve a harder problem: getting **any** status
information in front of a user at all when the plugin runs under a
frontend that isn't OpenCode's own TUI -- notably **JetBrains AI
Assistant via ACP** (Agent Client Protocol), one of this plugin's
actual deployment targets. Those are two different problems addressed
in the two sections below.

## 1. Tool-call telemetry (OpenTelemetry + in-memory summary)

See [ADR-0011](adr/0011-otel-bring-your-own-backend-telemetry.md) for
the full decision record. Summary:

- `tool.execute.before`/`tool.execute.after` plugin hooks
  (`src/telemetry/telemetry.ts`) observe **every** tool call in a
  session -- native `grep`/`glob` included, not just this
  plugin's own tools.
- Every observed call is dual-written to:
  - an **in-memory summary**, exposed via the `ai_context_telemetry_report` native
    tool as JSON (per-tool call count, total/average duration,
    approximate input/output token counts) -- zero configuration
    required;
  - a standard **OpenTelemetry span** (`tool.execute:<toolName>`) and a
    **duration histogram** (`opencode.tool.duration`, ms), via
    `@opentelemetry/api`'s global tracer/meter.
- The OTel path is **API-only** -- this plugin does not bundle an SDK
  or exporter. Per the OTel API's own design, calling a tracer/meter
  with no SDK registered is a safe no-op. If the OpenCode host process
  (or the user's environment more broadly) already has an OTel SDK +
  exporter configured, this plugin's spans/metrics show up there
  automatically, with zero plugin-side configuration. If not, the calls
  cost effectively nothing and produce no output.

### Built-in OTLP metrics export (opt-in)

Off by default. When enabled, the plugin creates its own `MeterProvider`
(not registered globally, so the host's OTel setup is untouched) and
pushes `opencode.tool.duration` over OTLP/HTTP to `<endpoint>/v1/metrics`.
A collector that is down only produces one warning; tool calls are never
affected.

| Env var | `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml` | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `AI_CONTEXT_OTEL_ENABLED` | `otel_enabled` | off |
| `AI_CONTEXT_OTEL_ENDPOINT` | `otel_endpoint` | `http://127.0.0.1:4318` |
| `AI_CONTEXT_OTEL_FLUSH_MS` | `otel_flush_ms` | `5000` |
| `AI_CONTEXT_PROJECT` | `project` | the worktree directory name (no hash) |
| `AI_CONTEXT_OTEL_SESSION_ID` | - | off (adds high-cardinality `sessionID` label) |

Metric: `opencode.tool.duration`, unit `ms`, histogram. Labels: `tool`,
`project` (also on the resource, with `service.name=ai-context`).
Prometheus-style backends expose it as
`opencode_tool_duration_milliseconds_{bucket,count,sum}` (or similar).

### How to actually see the OTel data

This plugin does not provide a collector or dashboard. To see spans/
metrics, register an SDK + exporter in the SAME process OpenCode itself
runs in (typically via `NODE_OPTIONS`/an OpenCode startup hook that
loads `@opentelemetry/sdk-node`, or whatever mechanism the OpenCode
host process already supports for its own instrumentation) pointed at
any OTLP-compatible backend (Jaeger, an OTel Collector, etc.). This
plugin's `trace.getTracer("ai-context-opencode-plugin")`/
`metrics.getMeter("ai-context-opencode-plugin")` calls will then be
picked up by that SDK like any other instrumented library in the
process.

### Instrumentation name and signals

| Signal | Name | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Span | `tool.execute:<toolName>` | Attributes: `tool`, `sessionID`, `callID` |
| Histogram | `opencode.tool.duration` | Unit `ms`; attributes `tool`, `sessionID` |
| `ai_context_telemetry_report` tool output | per-tool `callCount`, `totalDurationMs`, `avgDurationMs`, `totalInputTokens`, `totalOutputTokens`, `totalTokens` | In-memory only, resets when the process restarts |

## 2. Getting plugin status in front of a user across frontends (TUI vs. ACP)

opencode plugins run under multiple frontends: opencode's own TUI, and
**ACP-based clients** (Zed, **JetBrains AI Assistant** -- one of this
plugin's real deployment targets) that talk to opencode over the Agent
Client Protocol. Status mechanisms that work in one do **not** work in
the other, and this matters directly for this plugin: if it ever needs
to surface a user-visible status ("model download in progress," "index
backup restored," a warning about a malformed backup file, etc.), the
mechanism has to work under JetBrains AI Assistant's ACP bridge, not
just opencode's own TUI.

The full investigation, with source-level citations against opencode's
actual code (not just its type definitions/docs), lives in
[`opencode-plugin-workarounds.md`](opencode-plugin-workarounds.md) --
this section is the short version; read that file for the "why" and
the copy-pasteable implementation.

### Quick reference: what actually reaches the user, by frontend

| Mechanism | opencode TUI | ACP (JetBrains AI Assistant, Zed) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `client.tui.showToast(...)` | ✅ Works | ❌ Confirmed dead end -- opencode's ACP event bridge has no `tui.toast.show` case |
| `client.app.log(...)` | ✅ Always lands in the log file | ✅ Always lands in the log file | 
| Injected chat message (`session.prompt` with `noReply: true`) | N/A | ❌ Confirmed dead end -- built as a `user`-role message; the ACP bridge only forwards `assistant`-role parts |
| `"permission.ask"` hook | Likely unwired even in the TUI -- see the workarounds doc | Likely unwired -- no `plugin.trigger(...)` call site found in opencode's permission path |
| **Native OS notification** (`osascript` / `notify-send`, spawned directly) | ✅ Works | ✅ **Works** -- entirely bypasses opencode's hook/event system, so it's frontend-agnostic by construction |

**Practical takeaway for this plugin**: `client.app.log(...)` is fine as
a cheap, always-available secondary channel (nobody's watching it by
default, but it's there for debugging). For anything a user actually
needs to notice under JetBrains AI Assistant/ACP, use a native OS
notification -- see the workarounds doc's §1e for the ready-to-use
`notifyOs()` implementation, including the injectable-runner pattern
needed to keep unit tests from spawning real `osascript`/`notify-send`
processes (§3 of that doc).

### Known opencode-side quirk: double bootstrap

opencode invokes plugin bootstrap **twice** per session (confirmed via
opencode's own logs showing the same `run=<id>` with two independent,
near-simultaneous bootstrap cycles) -- this is opencode-side, not
something a plugin can fix. Any one-shot, user-visible side effect
(e.g. a "plugin loaded" OS notification) needs a time-windowed dedup
gate in front of it, or the user sees it fire twice for what feels like
one session start. See the workarounds doc §2 for the `OsNotifyGate`
pattern (`createOsNotifyGate`) this plugin should use if/when it adds
any bootstrap-time user-visible notification.

### Current status in this plugin

The plugin emits native OS notifications (plugin started; large indexing
run started/finished; indexing failed; `os_notifications: false` or
`AI_CONTEXT_OS_NOTIFICATIONS=0` silences them) but no chat-visible status
messages. Indexing progress (see
[ADR-0018](adr/0018-indexing-progress-via-status-file-and-tool-responses.md))
reaches the user through channels that work under ACP. `total` counts only files that need work; `reasons` says why (`new`, `changed`, `removed`, `upgrade`, `repair`, `summaries`; a forced `reindex_chunks`/`reindex_summaries` run counts as `upgrade`). Self-healing runs (`upgrade`/`repair`/`summaries`) always get an "Updating index" popup naming the reason, see [ADR-0027](adr/0027-self-healing-reindex.md):

Further files sit next to the status file (both git-ignored, written only when the plugin is enabled):

- **`index-tree.md`**: tree of every indexed file with language and chunk count, plus export date, repository, git branch/commit and last index update, and the files that failed. Written by `ai_context_export_index_tree` and after each completed indexing run.
- **`tool.log.md`** (opt-in, `tool_log: true`): one entry per tool call with time, tool, session/call id and arguments, followed by a `↳` entry with the duration and a response summary (size, result counts, first paths, error text, "empty result"). `tool_log_full_responses: true` logs complete arguments and the complete response text, without any truncation. At 5 MB the file is rotated to `tool.<time>.log.md` (newest 10 kept). Use it to see why an agent chose or misused a tool.
- **`error.log.md`**: persistent log of everything that went wrong (every problem that also becomes an OS popup, each failed file with its error, a failed run). Newest entries last, capped at 256 KB (oldest dropped). Unlike popups it is not deduplicated, so it shows how often something fails.

1. **Status file** `.opencode/ai-context/index-status.json`, rewritten at

# Writing and verifying an OpenCode 2.x plugin

Findings from porting this plugin to OpenCode 2.x (see also
[ADR-0031](adr/0031-opencode-2x-entry-and-search-steering.md)). Use the checklist
at the end to verify any other plugin.

Docs: <https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins/server> and
<https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/tools>.

## 1. Tools are hidden behind Code Mode by default

**Symptom.** The plugin registers fine and every tool works, but the agent cannot
call them directly. They only exist inside the `execute` tool
(`await tools.<name>({...})`), and the Code Mode catalog is *partial*: some tools
are not listed and need `search({ query: "<name>" })` to find their signature.
Agents then fall back to grep/glob or conclude the tools are missing.

**Cause.** In 2.x a tool added with `ctx.tool.transform(editor => editor.add(...))`
has `options: { namespace?, codemode? }`. MCP tools are documented to be reached
through `execute` unless `codemode: false`. The docs do not state the default for
plugin tools, but a plugin tool without `options` showed exactly this behaviour.
1.x plugin tools were always direct, so a straight port regresses silently.

**Fix.** Set `options: { codemode: false }` on the tools the agent should see
every turn. Direct tools cost prompt tokens on each request (their schemas are
sent every time), so keep rarely used or admin tools in Code Mode
(`codemode: true`). Here: `semantic_search`, `find_symbol`, `repo_structure`, `analyze_impact`,
`search_docs` and `index_status` are direct (`index_status` is what the agent
checks when results look empty, so it must be reachable without detours); the
seven `ai_context_*` admin tools stay in Code Mode (`DIRECT_TOOLS` in
`src/hook/v2-plugin.ts`).

**Steer the agent.** If any tools stay in Code Mode, say so in the system prompt
hint: which tools are direct, that the rest need `execute`, and that
`search(...)` returns a signature for an unlisted tool. Never tell the agent to
"call X" without saying how it is reachable.

## 2. Other 1.x to 2.x differences that matter

| Area | 1.x | 2.x |
|---|---|---|
| Entry | `Plugin` function returning hooks | `Plugin.define({ id, setup(ctx) })`; `setup` may return a cleanup function |
| Tool schema | zod `args` | JSON Schema `input` (`z.toJSONSchema(..., { io: "input" })`) |
| Tool result | string | `{ content: string \| parts[] }`; validate input yourself |
| Registration | `tool` map | `ctx.tool.transform(editor => editor.add(...))`; transforms are synchronous and replayed, so resolve async data first |
| Tool hooks | `tool.execute.before/after` | `ctx.tool.hook("execute.before" / "execute.after")`; the `after` event carries `status`, `result` or `error` |
| System prompt | `experimental.chat.system.transform` | `ctx.session.hook("context")`, push to `event.system` |

## 3. How to verify a plugin on 2.x (from inside a 2.x session)

Reload the plugin (`/reload`, or restart) and then check:

1. **Registered.** `await search({ query: "<plugin tool name>" })` inside
   `execute` finds every tool and returns its signature.
2. **Visible as intended.** Direct tools appear as normal tool calls. Everything
   else appears in the Code Mode catalog. Confirm with the tool list the session
   shows; the Code Mode catalog changes after a reload.
3. **Works.** Call each tool with a cheap, safe input and check the result is
   correct, not just non-empty. Skip destructive tools; they share the same
   registration path.
4. **Invalid input.** Call one tool with a wrong argument and confirm it returns
   a clear error instead of throwing.
5. **Hooks fire.** Do an edit/grep/read, then check whatever the hooks record
   (here: `ai_context_telemetry_report` lists those calls).
6. **Prompt steering.** Check the injected system text names the right tools and
   says how to reach them.
7. **Cleanup.** Reloading must not leave duplicate subscriptions or workers.

## 4. Checklist

- [ ] Entry uses `Plugin.define({ id, setup })` with a stable `id`.
- [ ] Tool `input` is valid JSON Schema without `$schema`.
- [ ] Each tool has an explicit `options.codemode` (do not rely on the default).
- [ ] Always-needed tools are `codemode: false`; admin/rare tools are in Code Mode.
- [ ] System prompt hint matches how each tool is reachable.
- [ ] Transform callbacks are synchronous and cheap; async work happens before.
- [ ] Hooks tolerate both `completed` and failed tool results.
- [ ] Nothing depends on 1.x-only features (global config, `lsp`, `file.edited`).
- [ ] Cleanup function aborts subscriptions and stops background work.
- [ ] Steps 1 to 7 above pass in a real 2.x session after `/reload`.

# Tool reference

The plugin registers native opencode tools (no MCP server, in-process

## Naming scheme ([ADR-0023](adr/0023-tool-naming-and-descriptions.md))

- **Research tools**, used by the agent while working, no prefix.
- **Admin tools**, used by the user on request, prefix `ai_context_`.

**OpenCode 2.x visibility.** The research tools plus `index_status` are listed directly. The
`ai_context_*` admin tools are only reachable in Code Mode: call them with `execute`
(`await tools.ai_context_rescan()`), and use `search({ query: "<name>" })` for a signature that is
not listed. On 1.x all tools are direct. See
[opencode-v2-plugin-checklist.md](opencode-v2-plugin-checklist.md).

## Research tools

| Tool | Use when | Arguments | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `repo_structure` | You are new to a project or area; replaces listing directories one by one | `dir_path?`, `depth?`, `project?` (name of another allowed project, no hash) | Directories first with file count and languages, then files |
| `semantic_search` | Conceptual question about **source code** ("where do we retry failed requests?") | `query`, `limit?` | Ranked chunks: path, line range, symbol, score, `project`; follow up with `read` on the line range |
| `analyze_impact` | Before changing, renaming or removing a function/class/method | `symbolName`, `path?`, `direction?` (callers/callees/both), `depth?`, `project?` (another allowed project) | Callers/callees/importers with file and line, plus `tests` (test files that import or call the symbol); edges are name-based, ambiguous ones flagged, confirm with `lsp` (1.x) or by reading the call site (2.x) |
| `find_symbol` | You know (part of) a class/function/method name and want its definition | `query`, `kind?`, `limit?`, `project?` (another allowed project) | Matches with path, line range, kind, container, plus `tests` (test files that import or call them); exact references via native `lsp` (1.x) or `analyze_impact` (2.x) |
| `search_docs` | Docs, ADRs, RFCs, design decisions (Markdown) | `query` (keywords), `mode?` (`toc_only`, `summary_only`, `node_text`), `limit?`, `project?` (another allowed project) | Matching sections from the document trees |
| `index_status` | Empty or partial results, or an `indexingNotice` in a response | `limit?` | File/chunk counts, newest `indexed_at`, recent changes, live progress, failed files |

`semantic_search` does not cover Markdown documents (they are stored as a tree,
not chunked); use `search_docs` for them. Results are fused from vector search and FTS5 BM25 (reciprocal rank fusion) and
re-ranked by a small cross-encoder (`reranker`). Chunks of type `file-summary`
describe a whole file. Exact identifiers: `find_symbol` or `grep`.

While an index run is active, results carry an `indexingNotice` so the agent
knows they may be incomplete.

## Data boundary

Tool results (code, document text, summaries) are returned to the agent and from there to its model provider, which may not be local. See [data-boundary.md](data-boundary.md).

## Steering the agent

Three layers, strongest first ([ADR-0020](adr/0020-steer-agent-to-context-tools.md)):

1. **System-prompt hint** (`agent_hint`): a short rule block appended through
   `experimental.chat.system.transform` (2.x: the `context` session hook; it also tells the agent which tools are direct and how to reach the Code Mode ones). It also maps "create an ai context backup" to `ai_context_export_backup` and "which files are indexed" to `ai_context_export_index_tree`. With `enabled` off (default) no tools and no hint are provided.
2. **Tool descriptions**: what the tool covers and does not, when to use it (in the words a user would say, e.g. "create an ai context backup"), what it returns, the next step. Destructive tools (`ai_context_delete_project`) tell the agent to confirm with the user first.
3. **Bundled skills**, on demand only: `index-status` (progress and tuning) and `cross-repo` (look into other indexed projects: `ai_context_list_projects` → `ai_context_allow_repo` → `project` argument).

Measure the effect with `ai_context_telemetry_report` (`view: "adoption"`).

# Troubleshooting

## The plugin does nothing / no tools in a repository

The plugin is opt-in per repository (ADR-0029). Check
`.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml`: `enabled` must be `true` (a missing key or a
malformed file counts as off), then restart opencode. `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_ENABLED`
overrides the file in both directions.

## Indexing seems stuck, fan is loud

Read `.opencode/ai-context/index-status.json` or call `index_status`.
`phase`: `idle | scanning | loading-model | indexing | done | failed`.
`loading-model` is the one-time model load. Lower `embed_threads`, exclude
generated code with `exclude:`, lower `embed_max_tokens` / `max_file_bytes`.
Live view: the bundled `index-status` skill ships `watch-index-status.sh`.

## Summaries are plain text and a popup says "API key not set"

The summary LLM answered HTTP 401. Export the key and restart opencode:
`export AI_CONTEXT_SUMMARY_LLM_API_KEY=<your key>` (or the variable named by
`api_key_env`). Then set `reindex_summaries: true` to rewrite the fallback
summaries now (they are also redone automatically on the next start). The same
hint is in `notices` of `index_status`.

## A second session starts indexing again

Since ADR-0025 only one process indexes a project (`index.lock` in the project
data directory); other sessions wait and skip files that are already indexed.
Sessions running an older plugin version ignore the lock: restart them.
A leftover lock of a crashed process is taken over after at most 45 s.

## Indexing failed with a memory message

The `max_memory_mb` guard stopped the run. Lower `embed_max_tokens` and
`max_file_bytes`, or raise `max_memory_mb`. See
[ADR-0019](adr/0019-bounded-memory-during-indexing.md).

## `ACP process exited unexpectedly. Exit code: 137` / `database is locked` in `Cache.db`

Exit 137 is an out-of-memory kill. The SQLite lock messages come from the
macOS HTTP cache of the host and are a symptom of memory pressure, not of this
plugin's stores. Look for stale `opencode acp` processes with high RSS
(`ps -axo pid,rss,command | grep opencode`) and end old ones by PID.
Expected: one `opencode acp` per session plus one embedding worker.

## Tool results are empty or partial

Indexing may still be running (`indexingNotice` in the response). Check
`index_status`. For Markdown documents use `search_docs`, not `semantic_search`.

## Agent still prefers grep

Check `agent_hint` is not disabled and look at the adoption view:
`ai_context_telemetry_report` with `view: "adoption"`. The system hook is
experimental in opencode; without it only tool descriptions apply.

## Shared worker problems

Log: `<data_dir>/embed-worker.log`. Socket: `<data_dir>/embed-worker.sock`.
Disable with `shared_worker: false` or `AI_CONTEXT_SHARED_WORKER=0`; the
plugin falls back to in-process embedding. A stale socket is replaced on the
next start.

## Old tool names

`ai_context_search_docs`, `ai_context_index_status` and `telemetry_report`
were renamed (ADR-0023) without aliases; update prompts and skills.

## Reset a project

`ai_context_delete_project` removes the stored index; it is rebuilt on the next
start (or restored from `.opencode/ai-context/backup/`).

## `Unknown or not allowed project`

A tool was called with `project: "<name>"` for a repo that is not on this
repo's allowlist. Use the `cross-repo` skill: `ai_context_list_projects` for the
exact `name` (no hash; a hashed key is not accepted), then
`ai_context_allow_repo`. It applies immediately. If the name is
missing from the list, that repo was never indexed with this plugin.

# AI agent workflow discipline

Applies to every session, always. Governs *how* the agent works, not
domain-specific code content (see the other rule files for that).

## 1. Plan before implementing

Before writing or modifying any code, produce a short implementation plan:
what will change, which files, in what order, and where the natural
commit/PR boundaries are. Wait for explicit confirmation before starting
implementation. Do not silently expand scope mid-implementation — if the
plan needs to change, say so and get confirmation before continuing.

## 2. Verify version-specific reality before acting, don't rely on memorized patterns

Training data mixes multiple versions of every library/framework. Before
touching a part of the stack, check the actual state in *this* repo
first — installed version (`package.json`/lockfile), current official
docs/changelog if uncertain — rather than defaulting to the most common
pattern in training data. Specifically check for:

- Known issues/breaking changes in the currently installed version.
- What's deprecated or should no longer be used, and its current
  replacement.
- Where a library/framework already replaces a language-native concept
  (e.g. a state library replacing ad-hoc Context+useState, a
  micro-frontend framework's own primitives replacing generic
  routing/event patterns) — default to the library's own idiom instead of
  the generic pattern trained on most.

If genuinely uncertain about current best practice for something
version-sensitive, say so explicitly rather than presenting a guess with
unwarranted confidence.

## 3. Small, isolated, reviewable increments

Each implementation step from the plan should be its own commit/PR-sized
unit. Do not bundle unrelated cleanup (e.g. "also removed some now
redundant code") into a feature change — propose it separately so it can
be reviewed and rolled back independently.

## 4. Tight verify-and-correct loop

After each change, run the relevant checks (tests/lint/build) before
moving to the next step, rather than batching many changes and checking
only at the end. React to failures immediately — fix and re-verify before
continuing, don't defer failures to a later cleanup pass.

For code changes: follow a test-driven workflow (write/update the failing
test first, then implement, then verify) — see
`.github/instructions/ai-context-tdd.instructions.md` and `docs/development.md`
(`npm run typecheck`, `npm run test:unit`).

## 5. Periodically propose reusable skills from the session

At natural checkpoints — end of a feature, end of a plan, or when a
workflow/terminal sequence repeats within the session — pause and ask:
"did this session use a workflow, script, or terminal sequence that
recurred or was fiddly enough to be worth turning into a reusable skill
(with a backing script)?" If yes, propose it explicitly rather than
letting the pattern silently repeat next time. Treat this as building a
persistent, versioned library of verified project skills over time, not
one-off note-taking.

## 6. Use minimal, relevant context

Don't pull in or reference more of the repo than the current task
actually needs. Prefer the scoped rule files (file-pattern/model-decision
triggered) over dumping unrelated context — excess irrelevant context
increases the risk of distraction and incorrect suggestions.

# Test-driven development for this plugin

Scope: any change under `src/` or `scripts/`. Reference: `docs/development.md`
(workflow, test conventions). All tests are unit tests in `test/unit/`
(`node:test` via tsx); there are no integration or e2e tiers and no Docker.

## 1. Red → green → refactor

For any behavior change (bug fix, new capability, refactor with an observable effect):

1. **Red**: write or update the test first. For a bug, reproduce it in a test
   and confirm it fails against the current code before fixing.
2. **Green**: implement the minimal change that makes it pass.
3. **Refactor**: clean up with the suite as safety net; re-run after each step.

Pure documentation/comment changes need no test. A new `config.yaml` key still
needs a test in `config-file.test.ts` (and `config-template.test.ts` if it is
in the template).

## 2. Commands

```bash
npm run typecheck                                              # tsc --noEmit
npm run test:unit                                              # full suite
node --import tsx --test test/unit/<name>.test.ts              # one file while iterating
```

A change is done when the new test failed before, passes after, and the **full**
`typecheck` + `test:unit` run is green. Run the full suite, not only the new
test, since neighbouring tests catch regressions.

## 3. Test conventions

- Name the test file after the module (`src/indexing/doc-tree-builder.ts` →
  `test/unit/doc-tree-builder.test.ts`).
- Stores use `:memory:` or temporary directories; embedders, workers, LLM
  `fetch` and notifiers are injected fakes. Never call a real model or server.
- `test:unit` already disables OS notifications, skill/project-file writing and
  the shared worker through env vars; don't rely on them being on.
- Tests that open timers or sockets must close them, or the run hangs.
- Changing tool names or descriptions requires updating
  `test/unit/tool-descriptions.test.ts`.

## 4. Don't hide a discovered bug

If a test reveals an unrelated pre-existing bug: don't silently adapt the
expectation and don't silently fix it (scope creep). Assert the current
behavior explicitly with a comment marking it a known gap, and list it under
"Known limitations" in `docs/status.md`.

## 5. Release

After code changes that should reach opencode, use the `plugin-release` skill
(typecheck, tests, build, install, restart).

## 6. Index-shape changes need a version bump

If a change alters what gets stored for an already indexed file (chunk
boundaries, chunk text, doc-tree structure or summaries), bump
`CODE_INDEX_VERSION` / `DOC_INDEX_VERSION` in `src/indexing/indexing.ts`, or
unchanged files keep the old shape (ADR-0027). If the embedded text or vector
format changes, bump `EMBED_FORMAT_VERSION` in `src/indexing/embed-input.ts`
instead (full re-index). Say in your summary which one you bumped.

first — installed version (`package.json`/lockfile), current official
docs/changelog if uncertain — rather than defaulting to the most common
pattern in training data. Specifically check for:

- Known issues/breaking changes in the currently installed version.
- What's deprecated or should no longer be used, and its current
  replacement.
- Where a library/framework already replaces a language-native concept
  (e.g. a state library replacing ad-hoc Context+useState, a
  micro-frontend framework's own primitives replacing generic
  routing/event patterns) — default to the library's own idiom instead of
  the generic pattern trained on most.

If genuinely uncertain about current best practice for something
version-sensitive, say so explicitly rather than presenting a guess with
unwarranted confidence.

## 3. Small, isolated, reviewable increments

Each implementation step from the plan should be its own commit/PR-sized
unit. Do not bundle unrelated cleanup (e.g. "also removed some now
redundant code") into a feature change — propose it separately so it can
be reviewed and rolled back independently.

## 4. Tight verify-and-correct loop

After each change, run the relevant checks (tests/lint/build) before
moving to the next step, rather than batching many changes and checking
only at the end. React to failures immediately — fix and re-verify before
continuing, don't defer failures to a later cleanup pass.

For code changes: follow a test-driven workflow (write/update the failing
test first, then implement, then verify) — see
`.github/instructions/ai-context-tdd.instructions.md` and `docs/development.md`
(`npm run typecheck`, `npm run test:unit`).

## 5. Periodically propose reusable skills from the session

At natural checkpoints — end of a feature, end of a plan, or when a
workflow/terminal sequence repeats within the session — pause and ask:
"did this session use a workflow, script, or terminal sequence that
recurred or was fiddly enough to be worth turning into a reusable skill
(with a backing script)?" If yes, propose it explicitly rather than
letting the pattern silently repeat next time. Treat this as building a
persistent, versioned library of verified project skills over time, not
one-off note-taking.

## 6. Use minimal, relevant context

Don't pull in or reference more of the repo than the current task
actually needs. Prefer the scoped rule files (file-pattern/model-decision
triggered) over dumping unrelated context — excess irrelevant context
increases the risk of distraction and incorrect suggestions.

# ADR-0001: Replace the Docker-based MCP server/watcher/LSP-bridge stack with a native OpenCode plugin

## Status

Accepted (2026-09). Implemented incrementally; see the sibling ADRs for
individual component decisions.

## Context

`.ai-context/` (the parent monorepo's original tooling) ran as a
multi-container Docker stack: a Postgres+Qdrant-backed MCP server
exposed over StreamableHTTP, a standalone file watcher container doing
continuous delta re-indexing, and an `lsp-bridge` container wrapping
several language servers (Python, Swift, clangd) behind a custom
protocol. All of this existed to give a coding agent semantic code
search, call/import-graph analysis, and long-document navigation.

By 2026, `sst/opencode` (the agent runtime this repo's users actually
run) had grown built-in equivalents for several of those
responsibilities: a native `lsp` tool with on-demand
`incomingCalls`/`outgoingCalls`/`findReferences`, native `grep`/`glob`,
a `skill` mechanism, and a first-class plugin API with `tool`,
`event`, and `config` hooks. Running a separate Docker stack alongside
an agent runtime that already covers much of the same ground meant:
extra operational surface (containers to start/keep healthy), a
network hop for every tool call (StreamableHTTP to a local server
instead of an in-process function call), and duplicate maintenance of
features OpenCode already had natively.

## Decision

Rebuild the *irreplaceable* differentiators -- hybrid semantic/keyword
code search and (opt-in) precomputed call/import-graph analysis -- as a
native OpenCode plugin (`ai-context-opencode-plugin/`), registered
directly via the plugin's `tool`/`event`/`config` hooks, with no MCP
server, no Docker, no separate watcher process. Everything OpenCode
already does well natively (`grep`, `glob`, on-demand `lsp` calls,
`skill` discovery) is deliberately NOT reimplemented; the plugin's
[`docs/architecture.md`](../architecture.md) documents this
overlap explicitly rather than leaving it implicit.

## Consequences

- No containers to run, start, or keep healthy for the core workflow;
  `npm install` + OpenCode picking up the plugin directory is the
  entire "install" step.
- Every plugin tool call is an in-process function call, not a network
  round trip -- removes an entire latency/failure-mode class (the
  StreamableHTTP transport, connection resets, "is the MCP server up"
  health checks).
- The plugin only fires while OpenCode is actually running a session
  -- there is no always-on watcher process. Re-indexing instead happens
  via (a) a one-off startup reconciliation walk when a session begins,
  and (b) `file.watcher.updated` events for the rest of the session.
  This trades "index is always fresh, even with OpenCode closed" for
  "no standing infrastructure" -- acceptable since the plugin's whole
  purpose is serving that same running OpenCode session.
- `lsp-bridge/` (the Python LSP client wrappers + its Dockerfile) was
  deleted entirely rather than ported, since its exact capability
  (on-demand call/reference lookups) is now covered natively by
  OpenCode's own `lsp` tool -- see ADR-0006.
- Losing: any capability that depended on the stack running
  independently of an active OpenCode session (e.g. a CI job querying
  the MCP server directly). None of this repo's current use cases
  needed that, so it wasn't preserved.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the Docker stack, add a thin plugin as a client of it.**
  Rejected: this keeps 100% of the operational overhead the rewrite
  was meant to remove, for a benefit (protocol reuse) that doesn't
  matter once nothing else consumes the MCP server directly.
- **Rewrite the MCP server in-process but keep it MCP-shaped (still a
  separate transport, just no Docker).** Rejected: OpenCode's plugin
  `tool` hook already IS the in-process registration mechanism; adding
  an MCP layer on top would be a transport nobody needs.

# ADR-0002: Embedded SQLite + brute-force cosine search instead of Postgres/Qdrant

## Status

Accepted (storage-spike, 2026-09).

## Context

The original stack used Postgres (structured metadata) + Qdrant (vector
search) as separate always-on services. Replacing the Docker
infrastructure (ADR-0001) meant the storage layer needed a genuinely
embedded, zero-server alternative -- something that lives inside the
plugin's own Node process with no separate service to start, healthy,
or connect to.

A storage spike measured `better-sqlite3` (synchronous, in-process,
file-backed) storing 768-dim vectors as BLOBs, with a v1 brute-force JS
cosine similarity scan (no ANN index) over all stored chunks per query.

## Decision

Use `better-sqlite3` as the sole storage backend
(`src/storage/vector-store.ts`), with brute-force cosine similarity in
JS for v1 -- no HNSW/IVF index, no separate vector database.

Measured search latency (768-dim vectors, brute-force scan):

| Chunk count | Latency |
| --- | --- |
| ~2,000 | ~110ms |
| ~10,000 | ~580ms |
| ~30,000 | ~1.75s |

This informs a tentative ~8,000-chunk threshold as a candidate cutover
point to a "heavy mode" Qdrant-backed path for very large monorepos --
**not yet implemented or validated against a real repo**; today the
plugin only has the SQLite path.

## Consequences

- Zero operational surface for storage: the `.sqlite` file lives under
  `~/.local/share/ai-context-opencode-plugin/projects/<key>/index.sqlite`,
  created/opened lazily by the plugin process itself.
- Search latency degrades linearly with chunk count since there's no
  ANN index -- acceptable for small/medium repos (the plugin's primary
  target), a real risk for very large monorepos once past roughly
  10-30k chunks.
- No externally-imposed schema/connection-pool/auth complexity that a
  real Postgres+Qdrant pair would require even for a single-user local
  tool.
- Left open, deliberately: a real "heavy mode" storage cutover (e.g.
  reintroducing Qdrant only past a measured chunk-count threshold) is
  future work, not yet built. `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_HEAVY_MODE` currently
  has no effect on storage at all (see ADR-0006's note on the flag's
  scope).

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep Qdrant, run it out-of-process.** Rejected outright by ADR-0001
  -- reintroduces the exact operational overhead being removed.
  Remains a candidate for a future "heavy mode" storage tier, not a
  wholesale replacement.
- **An embedded vector index library (e.g. an HNSW binding) instead of
  brute-force.** Deferred rather than rejected: added complexity
  (another native binding, index-rebuild-on-write semantics) wasn't
  justified until real usage shows brute-force scanning is actually a
  problem for this plugin's typical repo sizes.

# ADR-0003: One SQLite file per project instead of a shared store with a project-key column

## Status

Accepted (multi-repo-isolation, 2026-09).

## Context

The original stack used one Qdrant *collection* per project as its
physical isolation boundary -- separate projects' vectors were never
comingled at the storage layer, regardless of application-level query
filtering. Moving to embedded SQLite (ADR-0002) needed an equivalent
isolation story: OpenCode plugins run against a single `worktree` per
session, but the same plugin installation is reused across every repo
a user opens with OpenCode.

## Decision

`src/storage/project-key.ts`'s `deriveProjectKey` derives a stable,
project-scoped key from the session's `worktree`, and each project
gets its **own SQLite file** under
`~/.local/share/ai-context-opencode-plugin/projects/<key>/index.sqlite`
(with a sibling `doc-trees.sqlite` for doc-tree data -- see ADR-0009).
There is no shared table with a `project_key` column that every query
must remember to filter by.

## Consequences

- Isolation is structural, not query-discipline-dependent: a bug that
  forgets a `WHERE project_key = ?` clause is architecturally
  impossible here, because there is no other project's data reachable
  from an open handle to one project's file.
- Cross-repo search (an explicit, opt-in exception -- see ADR-0007's
  sibling `cross-repo-allowlist` feature) has to explicitly open
  *multiple* store handles and merge results in application code,
  rather than adding a query filter -- a deliberate trade-off: the
  common case (single-repo isolation) is free of a whole bug class, at
  the cost of cross-repo search being slightly more code.
- `src/storage/project-registry.ts` + the `ai_context_list_projects`/
  `ai_context_delete_project` tools exist because, unlike a shared
  store, deleting a project's data is now "delete a directory," which
  nothing does automatically when a repo falls out of use --
  reclaiming disk space is a manual, explicit action.
- The store's file path always lives OUTSIDE the project's own
  worktree (under the user's local data dir, not inside the repo) --
  this is also why the plugin's own writes never re-trigger its own
  `file.watcher.updated` indexing (see ADR-0012): OpenCode only watches
  the worktree, and the store file isn't in it.

## Alternatives considered

- **A single shared SQLite file with a `project_key` column on every
  row.** Rejected: reintroduces exactly the "every query must
  remember to filter" risk this decision exists to avoid, for a
  marginal simplicity gain (one file to manage instead of N) that
  doesn't matter much given SQLite files are cheap and self-contained.

# ADR-0004: Hand-rolled `onnxruntime-node` embedding pipeline instead of the npm `fastembed` package

## Status

Accepted, corrects an earlier plan (2026-09-15 audit).

## Context

The plugin needs an in-process embedding backend for
`nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5` (chosen for its Matryoshka-truncatable
output and permissive license). The initial plan was to depend on the
npm `fastembed` package, since it promises exactly this: bundled ONNX
models + tokenization + pooling behind a simple `EmbeddingModel` API.

A pre-implementation audit (recorded in the session's `plan.md`,
"Auditing fastembed/nomic embedding fit") found two disqualifying
problems:

1. `fastembed`'s `EmbeddingModel` catalog **does not include nomic at
   all** -- there's no supported model identifier for
   `nomic-embed-text-v1.5`.
2. Even setting that aside, `fastembed`'s `getEmbeddings()` extraction
   is **hardcoded to the first token position (CLS pooling)**, not the
   attention-mask-weighted mean pooling `nomic-embed-text-v1.5` was
   actually trained with. Using it would silently produce degraded
   embeddings with no error -- the worst kind of failure for a
   retrieval-quality-sensitive feature.

Forking `fastembed-js` to add nomic support and fix pooling was also
considered and rejected: it would mean maintaining a fork of someone
else's abstraction for behavior that's actually quite small once
manually implemented.

## Decision

Hand-roll the embedding pipeline directly:

- `src/embedding/embedder.ts` implements the actual math this
  decision requires owning: attention-mask-weighted mean pooling
  (`meanPool`), L2 normalization (`l2Normalize`), and Matryoshka
  dimension truncation (`truncateMatryoshka`) -- injectable
  `tokenize`/`runInference` dependencies keep this module free of real
  I/O in unit tests.
- `src/embedding/model-runtime.ts` provides the REAL implementation of
  those two dependencies: `onnxruntime-node` for inference, the
  official `tokenizers` package for tokenization, and
  `@huggingface/hub`'s `downloadFileToCacheDir` for fetching the
  quantized ONNX export (`onnx/model_quantized.onnx`, ~137MB int8 vs.
  ~547MB fp32) and tokenizer config.
- `createLazyEmbedder` loads the tokenizer + ONNX session once, lazily
  (on first real `semantic_search`/indexing call, not at plugin
  startup), and shares that single loaded session between
  `embedQuery` and `embedDocument`.

Verified manually end-to-end (real download + real ONNX inference, not
part of the fast unit suite): the model's ONNX graph takes
`input_ids`/`token_type_ids`/`attention_mask` and returns a single
`last_hidden_state` output of shape `[1, seqLen, 768]`; L2 norm of the
resulting embedding was confirmed ≈ 1.

## Consequences

- No dependency on an abstraction whose model catalog and pooling
  strategy don't match this plugin's actual model -- the tradeoff is
  owning ~100 lines of pooling/normalization/truncation math directly,
  which is small and now unit-tested (`embedder.test.ts`).
- The int8-quantized model export is a deliberate quality/size
  trade-off: negligible retrieval-quality loss for a ~4x smaller
  download, matching the plugin's "no bundled heavy infra, keep it
  light" philosophy.
- Lazy loading means the first `semantic_search` call (or first
  indexing pass) in a session pays the model-load cost, not every
  OpenCode session start -- deliberate, since `semantic_search` may
  never be called in a given session.
- See ADR-0005 for the model *cache location* decision (a related but
  separate choice from the pipeline implementation itself).

## Alternatives considered

- **npm `fastembed` package as originally planned.** Rejected: wrong
  model catalog, wrong pooling strategy (silent quality degradation).
- **Forking `fastembed-js`.** Rejected: maintaining a fork for a
  relatively small amount of actual logic isn't worth the ongoing
  upstream-drift maintenance cost.
- **`@huggingface/transformers` (transformers.js).** Considered in the
  same audit as a heavier-but-more-complete alternative; not chosen
  because the plugin only needs a single fixed pipeline (tokenize ->
  ONNX inference -> pool -> normalize -> optionally truncate), which
  is small enough to own directly with narrower, more auditable
  dependencies (`onnxruntime-node` + `tokenizers` directly, rather than
  a larger all-in-one library).

# ADR-0005: Download the embedding model into Hugging Face's shared cache, not a plugin-private directory

## Status

Accepted (port-semantic-search-tool, 2026-09).

## Context

The embedding pipeline (ADR-0004) needs to download and cache a ~137MB
quantized ONNX model plus its tokenizer config. The download uses
`@huggingface/hub`'s `downloadFileToCacheDir`, which accepts an
optional `cacheDir` parameter. If left unset, it uses the SAME standard
shared cache location (`$HF_HOME/hub`, `~/.cache/huggingface/hub` by
default) that Python's `huggingface_hub`/`transformers`/
`sentence-transformers` and JS's `@huggingface/transformers` all use.

The user separately runs (or may run) other OpenCode plugins that also
embed with `nomic-embed-text-v1.5` or other HF-hosted models.

## Decision

Leave `cacheDir` unset by default (`resolveModelCacheDir` returns
`undefined` unless overridden), so the download lands in HF's own
standard shared, content-addressed cache rather than a
plugin-private directory. `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_MODEL_CACHE_DIR` remains
as an explicit opt-out for locked-down/air-gapped setups that want a
private, fully plugin-owned cache instead.

## Consequences

- If another OpenCode plugin (or any other HF-ecosystem tool on the
  same machine) also embeds with `nomic-embed-text-v1.5`, it downloads
  the exact same content-addressed blob once, and every consumer
  reuses it -- no duplicate ~137MB downloads per plugin.
- This is deliberately DIFFERENT from the per-project vector-store
  files (ADR-0003): the model is shared, static, non-project-specific
  data, so there's no isolation benefit to duplicating it the way
  per-project data must be kept separate.
- A user on a locked-down/air-gapped machine, or one who wants strict
  per-plugin disk isolation for any reason, can still force a private
  cache via `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_MODEL_CACHE_DIR` without any code
  changes.

## Alternatives considered

- **A plugin-private cache directory by default (e.g. under
  `~/.local/share/ai-context-opencode-plugin/models/`).** Rejected as
  the default: guarantees duplicate downloads across independently
  developed plugins using the same public model, for no isolation
  benefit, since the artifact itself has no per-project or per-plugin
  sensitive content.

# ADR-0006: `analyze_impact` backed by a precomputed symbol/import/call graph, always on

## Status

Accepted, revised (2026-09). Supersedes the earlier "opt-in heavy mode,
then un-register until real" decisions recorded below under History.

## Context

The original stack's MCP server exposed `analyze_impact`: a precomputed,
repo-wide call/import graph. Slimming the plugin first gated it behind
`AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_HEAVY_MODE`, then (critical-review finding
"analyze-impact-honest-stub") un-registered it, because its `execute()`
always threw "not implemented yet" -- there was no graph behind it, and a
visible tool that always fails is worse than an absent one.

Those decisions assumed the graph needed heavy infrastructure. It does
not: with tree-sitter already in the plugin (ADR-0013, ADR-0016) and an
embedded SQLite store (ADR-0002), a static graph is cheap to build during
the normal indexing pass.

## Decision

`analyze_impact` is **always registered** and answers from a graph kept
in its own SQLite file (`graph.sqlite`, next to the vector store):

- **Tables** (`storage/graph-store.ts`): `graph_files`, `symbols`,
  `import_edges`, `call_edges`.
- **Extraction** (`indexing/graph/`): one tree-sitter parse per file
  yields symbols, imports and calls for TypeScript/JavaScript, Python,
  Java, Kotlin, C#, Go, Rust, Ruby, C and C++.
- **Resolution** (`import-resolver.ts`, `call-resolver.ts`): imports are
  resolved to repo files; calls are matched by name and narrowed by
  same-file, imported-file, receiver and directory evidence.
- **Indexing** (`graph-indexer.ts`, hooked into `createIndexer`): files
  are stored raw per update and edges are re-resolved once per batch,
  only for what the batch could have changed. Graph failures never block
  chunk indexing.
- **Framework edges** (`framework-extractor.ts`, TS/JS only), reported
  with an edge `kind`: React JSX component usage (`jsx`), Angular
  constructor/`@Inject`/`inject()` references (`inject`), NgModule and
  standalone-component metadata arrays (`decorator`), and selector usage
  in inline templates (`template`). `selector:` values become `selector`
  symbols on their class; a template edge keeps the raw tag in
