  `qualifier` and is re-pointed at the owning class whenever selectors
  change, so the component's callers include the templates using it.
  Templates in `templateUrl` files are not analysed.
- **Backup**: `.opencode/ai-context/backup/graph.jsonl`, exported by
  `ai_context_export_backup`, restored on startup when the graph is empty.
- **Ambiguity**: edges that cannot be tied to one definition are flagged
  `ambiguous`. The tool's `hint` tells the agent to confirm them with the
  native `lsp` tool (`goToDefinition` at the call site, `findReferences`
  at the definition), with file:line locations.

`heavyMode` / `isHeavyModeEnabled()` no longer gates anything and has no
functional effect; it stays as plumbing for a future heavy-mode feature.

## Consequences

- Framework edges are heuristic: JSX tags are matched by name, and
  template attributes only when camelCase (to skip `class`, `id`, ...).
- The graph is static and name-based: no type information, no
  tsconfig `paths`, Gradle source roots, Cargo workspaces or Go module
  names in import resolution, and calls inside anonymous callbacks have no
  named caller. Precision is bounded by that; `lsp` remains the exact
  answer, and the tool says so.
- Indexing does slightly more work per file (one extra parse), and the
  graph adds one more file to the per-project data directory.
- The native `lsp` tool is still what callers should use for exact,
  type-aware results; `analyze_impact` saves round trips, it does not
  replace it.
- `.ai-context/lsp-bridge/` stays deleted: the native `lsp` tool covers
  its capability.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep it opt-in behind heavy mode.** Rejected: the graph is cheap and
  an agent benefits on any repo size.
- **Keep it unregistered and rely on `lsp` only.** Rejected: many
  sequential `lsp` queries are slow for "what does changing X affect".
- **Type-aware resolution via LSP at index time.** Rejected for now:
  needs language servers running during indexing; instead ambiguity is
  surfaced and left to the agent's on-demand `lsp` calls.

## History

- Initial: gate `analyze_impact` behind `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_HEAVY_MODE`
  (`slim-analyze-impact-drop-lspbridge`).
- Revised: un-register entirely because `execute()` was a stub
  (`analyze-impact-honest-stub`).
- Revised (this version): real implementation, always on.

# ADR-0007: Commit-able, repo-local JSONL backup instead of a database dump/service

## Status

Amended by [ADR-0028](0028-compact-sharded-backup.md): the chunk backup is now sharded `index-NNNN.jsonl` files with float16 vectors.

Accepted (repo-local-backup; extended by doc-tree-backup and
validate-backup-import-schema, 2026-09).

## Context

Per-project data (ADR-0003) lives outside the project's own worktree,
in the user's local data directory -- which means a fresh clone of a
repo (or a new teammate's machine) starts with an EMPTY index and has
to pay the full re-indexing cost (chunking + embedding every file)
before `semantic_search`/`search_docs` become useful. The
original stack's Postgres+Qdrant pair had no equivalent "ship the
index with the repo" story either -- an out-of-band export was outside
its normal operating mode.

## Decision

`src/storage/backup.ts` exports the vector store as sorted JSON Lines
to `.opencode/ai-context/backup/index.jsonl` **inside the worktree**
(the opposite placement from the live per-project store) -- making it
commit-able and git-diffable (stable key order per row, sorted by
`relativePath`, so re-exporting an unchanged store produces a
byte-identical diff). A sibling `doc-trees.jsonl` in the same directory
covers `DocTreeStore`'s PageIndex-style Markdown trees (ADR-0009) the
same way, as a separate file so the two backups stay independently
diffable and a repo with no tree-indexed Markdown never gets an empty
doc-trees file created.

On plugin startup, if the current machine's local store (chunks, or
doc trees, checked independently) is empty, the corresponding backup
file is auto-imported -- never overwriting a store that already has
local data. The `ai_context_export_backup` tool triggers a fresh
export of both backups on demand, e.g. before committing.

## Consequences

- A fresh clone (or new teammate) gets a working, populated index
  immediately after `git pull`, with no re-indexing wait, as long as
  someone committed a reasonably fresh backup.
- Both backup files are ordinary git-tracked text files -- diffable,
  mergeable in the git sense. A committed backup can also arrive
  corrupted the same way any tracked file can (most commonly an
  unresolved git merge conflict, or a hand-edited/partially-written
  row) -- `importBackup`/`importDocTreeBackup` parse and shape-validate
  each row independently and silently skip any row that fails either
  step (a `JSON.parse` failure, a missing required field, or a
  wrong-typed field such as `vector`/`nodes` not being an array),
  rather than letting one bad line abort the entire import
  (validate-backup-import-schema, closed).
- This is an entirely manual, on-demand action (the tool), not an
  automatic side effect of every indexing event -- committing an index
  snapshot is a deliberate "share this with the team" decision, not
  background noise on every save.
- Because doc-tree and chunk backups are separate files with
  independent empty-store checks, a repo can have one without the
  other (e.g. all code, no long-form Markdown) without an artifact
  being created for the unused half.

## Alternatives considered

- **A single merged backup file covering both chunks and doc trees.**
  Rejected: would force every backup update to touch one file
  regardless of which half actually changed, and would create an
  artifact for doc trees even in repos with no long-form Markdown.
- **No backup at all; re-index on every fresh clone.** Rejected as the
  default: acceptable for a single active developer, but every new
  clone/teammate/CI checkout would otherwise pay the full re-indexing
  cost from zero, with no way to share that cost across a team.

# ADR-0008: Enforce `.gitignore` + an extension safelist at both indexing entry points

## Status

Accepted (repo-walker-ignore-filtering, critical-review follow-up,
2026-09).

## Context

The original `.ai-context` stack's `watcher/indexer.py` combined two
filtering mechanisms before ever reading a file's content:

1. A merged `pathspec` built from the worktree's own `.gitignore` (plus
   configured extra gitignore files).
2. `config.yaml`'s `include_extensions` -- an explicit SAFELIST of
   extensions, which doubles as the binary-detection mechanism ("this
   is also what keeps binaries out -- no separate binary-detection step
   needed," per that file's own comment) rather than sniffing file
   contents.

The plugin's initial `repo-walker.ts` implementation had neither: only
a small hardcoded directory denylist (`node_modules`, `.git`, `dist`,
etc.). A critical review of the implementation flagged this as a real
gap, not a cosmetic one: without both mechanisms, every file not caught
by that small denylist -- images, archives, lockfiles, `.env`, vendored
binaries, anything a project-specific `.gitignore` excludes -- would be
read as UTF-8, chunked, embedded, and (via ADR-0007's repo-local
backup) potentially committed into git as a leaked artifact.

## Decision

`src/indexing/file-filter.ts` ports both mechanisms:

- `isIndexableExtension` -- a safelist mirroring `config.yaml`'s
  `include_extensions` (plus `INDEXABLE_FILENAMES` for the one
  extensionless entry, `Dockerfile`).
- `createIgnoreMatcher`/`loadGitignoreSync` -- real `.gitignore`
  semantics (including negation patterns like `!important.log`) via the
  `ignore` npm package, rather than hand-rolled glob matching.
- `createFileFilter` combines both into the single predicate the
  indexing pipeline needs.

Critically, this filter is wired into BOTH indexing entry points, not
just one:

1. `repo-walker.ts`'s startup full-repo walk.
2. `indexing.ts`'s `indexOneFile`, via a new optional `shouldIndexFile`
   dependency -- so `file.watcher.updated`-driven incremental changes
   (edits made during a live session) get identical filtering. Without
   this second wiring, a binary or gitignored file edited mid-session
   would bypass the startup walk's filter entirely.

The `shouldIndexFile` check runs BEFORE `readFile` in `indexOneFile`,
so a rejected file's content is never even read -- and it runs AFTER
the existing `deleteChunksForFile`/`deleteTree` calls, so a file that
becomes newly-excluded (e.g. just added to `.gitignore`) still gets its
previously-indexed chunks/tree cleaned up correctly.

## Consequences

- Binaries, secrets (`.env`), and vendored/generated files are no
  longer read, chunked, embedded, or risked in the committed backup
  (ADR-0007).
- The filter must be remembered at every future indexing entry point --
  the two-place wiring here is not incidental; any new way of feeding
  files into the pipeline needs the same `shouldIndexFile` check.
- A file that becomes newly gitignored (or newly excluded by an
  extension change) during a live session is correctly de-indexed on
  its next `file.watcher.updated` event, not just skipped going
  forward.

## Alternatives considered

- **Content-sniffing binary detection (e.g. checking for null bytes)
  instead of an extension safelist.** Rejected: diverges from the
  original stack's proven approach, and an explicit safelist is more
  predictable/auditable than heuristic content sniffing.
- **Hand-rolled `.gitignore` glob matching.** Rejected: `.gitignore`
  semantics (negation, directory-only patterns, anchoring) are
  easy to get subtly wrong; the `ignore` npm package is a small,
  zero-dependency, widely used implementation, consistent with this
  plugin's "no bundled heavy infra, keep it light" philosophy.

# ADR-0009: PageIndex-style hierarchical indexing for long-form Markdown, mutually exclusive with chunking

## Status

Accepted (port-doc-tree-markdown, 2026-09).

## Context

The original stack (`watcher/doc_tree_builder.py` + `mcp-server/src/
doc_tree.ts`) treated long-form Markdown (docs, ADRs, wikis) differently
from source code: instead of paragraph/semantic chunking, it parsed the
document's heading structure into a tree and let an agent navigate it
top-down (table of contents -> node summary -> full node text) --
inspired by the PageIndex approach
(https://github.com/VectifyAI/PageIndex) of reasoning-based retrieval
over a document's own hierarchical structure, rather than flat
similarity search over arbitrary-sized chunks. `chunker.py` gated which
files got this treatment vs. ordinary chunking.

## Decision

Port this as its own path, not a chunker variant:

- `src/indexing/doc-tree-builder.ts` -- `parseMarkdownHeadings` /
  `buildDocTree` / `shouldUseTreeIndex` (the gate deciding whether a
  file is tree-indexed instead of chunked -- mutually exclusive per
  file, matching the original's gate).
- `src/storage/doc-tree-store.ts` -- persists trees in their own SQLite
  file, sibling to the vector store, same per-project directory
  (ADR-0003's isolation applies here too).
- `src/search/doc-tree-search.ts` -- ports `buildToc`/`searchDocTrees`
  (keyword-based node scoring); a `limit` on files returned replaces
  the original's `tokenBudget`, since that fed the original's
  `assembleContext` orchestrator, which this plugin never wired up (no
  equivalent orchestration layer exists here).
- `src/tools/search-docs.ts` exposes it as `search_docs`
  with three modes (`toc_only`/`summary_only`/`node_text`), letting the
  agent progressively drill down instead of getting a flat text blob.

## Consequences

- Long-form docs get structure-aware retrieval (agent can ask for just
  the TOC, then a specific node's summary, then its full text) instead
  of being chunked into arbitrary paragraph-sized pieces that lose the
  document's own organization.
- Because tree-indexing and chunking are mutually exclusive per file,
  every Markdown file is either fully tree-indexed or fully chunked --
  never both -- avoiding duplicate/conflicting representations of the
  same content.
- The doc-tree backup gap (a file separate from the chunk backup not
  covering doc trees at all) was a real critical-review finding, since
  fixed -- see ADR-0007's description of the sibling `doc-trees.jsonl`
  file.
- pandoc-based conversion of non-Markdown document formats (`.docx`
  etc.) into this same tree-indexing pipeline was discussed as a
  future extension but is NOT implemented -- today only Markdown files
  get tree-indexed; other formats are either chunked (if
  extension-safelisted, see ADR-0008) or skipped entirely.

## Update (2026-10-08)

- Every `.md` file is tree-indexed; the former 8-heading threshold is gone
  (`minHeadingsForTree` now defaults to 0), so documents are never chunked.
  A file without headings becomes one root node titled with its path.
- Node and document summaries are written at index time by the `summary_llm`
  server (same client and failure handling as file summaries, own prompt).
  Without a reachable server they stay `null` and ranking uses titles only.

## Alternatives considered

- **Treat Markdown as just another chunkable file type.** Rejected:
  loses the document's own hierarchical structure, which is
  specifically valuable for docs/ADRs/wikis where an agent benefits
  from navigating top-down rather than getting arbitrary paragraph
  chunks ranked by similarity alone.
- **Full PageIndex-style LLM-driven tree construction (using an LLM to
  decide the tree structure, per the original PageIndex project).**
  Not adopted: the ported version uses the document's own heading
  structure directly (deterministic, no extra LLM calls needed), which
  is sufficient for well-structured Markdown docs and keeps this
  feature free of an additional LLM-call dependency.

# ADR-0011: OpenTelemetry API-only telemetry ("bring your own backend"), dual-written with an in-memory summary

## Status

Accepted (otel-telemetry, telemetry-hooks, 2026-09).

## Context

OpenCode's `tool.execute.before`/`tool.execute.after` plugin hooks fire
for EVERY tool call in a session -- native `grep`/`glob`/`lsp` calls
included, not just this plugin's own tools. That's automatic,
zero-self-instrumentation telemetry: unlike the originating monorepo's
`bench.js` CLI (external tooling, not part of this package, which
requires an agent to manually wrap/start/stop each action it wants
measured), these hooks see everything without the agent doing anything
special.

The question was what to DO with that telemetry: build/bundle a full
observability stack (an exporter, a local collector, a persistence
layer), or something lighter.

## Decision

Dual-write telemetry from a single recorder
(`src/telemetry/telemetry.ts`):

1. **An in-memory summary** -- zero-config, exposed via the
   `ai_context_telemetry_report` tool as JSON (per-tool call count, total/average
   duration, and approximate input/output token counts, using the same
   word/number/punctuation-run token approximation as `bench.js`, kept
   numerically consistent on purpose so results are comparable across
   both).
2. **Standard OpenTelemetry spans + a duration histogram**, via
   `@opentelemetry/api` -- **API only, no bundled SDK or exporter**.

Per the OTel API's own design, calling a tracer/meter with no SDK
registered is a safe no-op. That means this plugin never needs to
bundle, configure, or manage an actual telemetry backend itself --
"bring your own backend," the same pattern already used for the
LLM/embedding model backend (ADR-0004/0005: this plugin picks a
default, but doesn't force infrastructure choices on the user).

## Consequences

- Zero-config users get the `ai_context_telemetry_report` tool's summary with no
  setup at all.
- Users who already run an OTel collector for their OpenCode host
  process get this plugin's tool-call spans/duration histogram
  automatically, for free, with no plugin-side configuration --
  they're using the exact same global tracer/meter providers
  `@opentelemetry/api` already exposes.
- Users with no OTel SDK configured pay effectively zero cost for the
  OTel code path (confirmed no-op by the API's own design), so there's
  no reason to feature-flag it off.
- This exposes the raw signal (spans, histogram, in-memory summary) for
  any future benchmarking or evaluation harness to consume, without this
  plugin needing to implement or own any benchmarking logic itself.
  (Benchmarking this plugin's own retrieval quality was considered and
  explicitly descoped from this project's own plan -- see `plan.md` --
  but the telemetry surface remains generically useful regardless of
  who consumes it.)

## Alternatives considered

- **Bundle a full OTel SDK + exporter (e.g. always export to a local
  OTLP endpoint).** Rejected: forces an infrastructure/configuration
  decision (where does telemetry go?) onto every user, even those who
  don't want it, and duplicates whatever OTel setup the user's
  OpenCode host process may already have.
- **In-memory summary only, no OTel at all.** Rejected: would lose the
  "automatic, zero-self-instrumentation" benefit for users who DO
  already have real observability infrastructure in place and would
  want this plugin's calls to show up in it.

# ADR-0012: React to `file.watcher.updated`, not `file.edited`, for re-indexing

## Status

Accepted (replace-watcher-with-hooks, 2026-09).

## Context

OpenCode exposes (at least) two distinct file-change signals a plugin
can subscribe to via its `event` hook: `file.edited` (fires only for
edits the agent itself made through its own tools, e.g. a `write`/`edit`
tool call) and `file.watcher.updated` (fires for changes from ANY
process -- external editors, `git pull`, another terminal, a build
step writing generated files).

The Docker-based watcher this plugin replaces (ADR-0001) watched the
filesystem directly, with no notion of "who" made a change -- it
re-indexed on any observed change, full stop.

## Decision

Subscribe to `file.watcher.updated`, not `file.edited`.

## Consequences

- Matches what the old watcher container actually needed to catch: a
  user editing files in their own editor outside of OpenCode, a `git
  pull`/branch switch, or any other external process touching the
  worktree, all trigger re-indexing -- not just changes the agent made
  through its own tool calls.
- If `file.edited` were used instead, external changes (the common
  case of a human editing code alongside the agent) would silently
  never re-trigger indexing, leaving the index stale relative to what's
  actually on disk without the agent (or the plugin) ever being aware.
- Combined with ADR-0003's placement of the store file OUTSIDE the
  worktree, this also means the plugin's own writes (to its SQLite
  files) never re-trigger `file.watcher.updated` on themselves --
  there's no risk of a self-triggering indexing loop.

## Alternatives considered

- **`file.edited`.** Rejected: too narrow -- would miss the exact class
  of external, non-agent-driven changes the original watcher was built
  to catch.
- **Both events.** Considered redundant: since `file.watcher.updated`
  is a superset covering everything `file.edited` would also catch (an
  agent's own edit is still a change on disk that the watcher observes
  too), listening to both would just double-fire without adding
  coverage.

# ADR-0013: `web-tree-sitter` (WASM) grammars for per-language chunking, not native bindings

## Status

Accepted (2026-09-16), for the `port-tree-sitter-chunker` follow-up.

## Context

`src/lib/chunker.ts` currently only ports the paragraph-based fallback
from the original stack's `watcher/chunker.py`; the ~1100 remaining
lines of that file are per-language, tree-sitter-boundary-aware chunking
for ~13 languages (Kotlin, TS/TSX, JS/JSX, Python, C#, Java, Swift, Go,
Rust, Ruby, PHP, C/C++, Vue) plus dedicated Markdown/SQL/YAML handling.
Bringing that over requires a real tree-sitter dependency, and there are
two ways to get one in Node:

1. **`node-tree-sitter` + native `tree-sitter-<lang>` npm packages** --
   the reference/most mature ecosystem, but each language package is a
   native addon requiring either a prebuilt binary for the exact
   OS/arch/Node-ABI combination or a local compile toolchain
   (`node-gyp`, a C compiler, Python) at install time.
2. **`web-tree-sitter`** -- tree-sitter's official WASM binding; each
   grammar ships as a `.wasm` file loaded at runtime, no native
   compilation step anywhere in the install path.

This plugin's install story so far has been "one native dependency,
already accepted and isolated" (`onnxruntime-node`, ADR-0004) -- adding
13 more native language-grammar packages on top of that would multiply
exactly the kind of install-time fragility (per-OS/arch/Node-ABI
prebuilt-binary mismatches, CI/sandboxed-environment compile failures)
the plugin has otherwise deliberately avoided by choosing SQLite over
Postgres/Qdrant (ADR-0002) and a hand-rolled embedding pipeline over a
heavier framework (ADR-0004).

## Decision

Use `web-tree-sitter` (WASM) for the per-language chunking grammars, not
native `tree-sitter-<lang>` bindings.

The known cost is per-file parse overhead: WASM tree-sitter parsing is
typically ~1.2-2x slower than the native binding, which is negligible
per-file but accumulates across a full initial index of a very large
repo. This plugin already has an explicit relief valve for that case --
"heavy mode" (`AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_HEAVY_MODE`, ADR-0006) hands very large
repos back to the original Docker stack's brute-force-at-scale
architecture -- so accepting a modest WASM indexing-time cost for
typical repo sizes, in exchange for install reliability across
platforms/CI/sandboxes, is consistent with that existing design rather
than a new tradeoff being introduced.

Each grammar's `.wasm` file is loaded lazily per language, mirroring the
lazy-load pattern already used for the embedding model (ADR-0004) --
parse trees for a given language are only needed once a file of that
language is actually chunked, not at plugin startup.

## Consequences

- No native compile step or prebuilt-binary matrix to maintain across
  ~13 additional language packages -- `npm install` stays reliable
  cross-platform, matching the existing `onnxruntime-node`-is-the-one-
  exception posture from ADR-0004.
- Modest per-file/aggregate parse-time cost vs. native bindings, most
  visible during a large repo's first full index -- acceptable given
  "heavy mode" already exists as the escape hatch for repos at that
  scale.
- Official prebuilt `.wasm` grammars don't exist (or aren't current)
  for every one of the ~13 target languages; a few may need building
  from source via `tree-sitter build --wasm` as part of this work,
  vendored alongside the plugin rather than fetched at runtime.
- `chunker.ts`'s existing paragraph-based `chunkText()` fallback remains
  the fallback for any language/file type without a wired-up grammar --
  this decision only changes how tree-sitter itself is obtained, not the
  fallback behavior.

## Alternatives considered

- **`node-tree-sitter` + native per-language npm packages.** Rejected:
  faster and a more complete/mature grammar ecosystem, but reintroduces
  exactly the native-dependency install fragility (per-OS/arch/Node-ABI
  prebuilt binaries or a local compile toolchain) this plugin has
  otherwise avoided; a real risk for CI and restricted/sandboxed
  environments specifically.
- **Skip tree-sitter chunking entirely, keep only the paragraph
  fallback.** Rejected: the whole point of AST-boundary-aware chunking
  (splitting on function/class boundaries rather than arbitrary
  paragraph breaks) is retrieval-quality-sensitive -- the original
  stack's `chunker.py` exists precisely because paragraph-only chunking
  produces worse `semantic_search` results for source code.

# ADR-0014: Team-shared `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml` with env-var override

## Status

Accepted (config-file feature, user-directed, 2026-09-16). Amended by [ADR-0029](0029-opt-in-enabled-flag-and-default-template.md): the generated file now carries every default as an active value, an `enabled` master switch (off by default) and no secrets; the separate example file was removed. Amended by [ADR-0030](0030-allowlist-in-config-yaml.md): the cross-repo allowlist is the `allowed_repos` key of this file.

## Context

By the time this decision was made, four settings existed, each
configurable ONLY via an `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_*` environment variable:
`AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR` (project-key.ts), `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_EMBED_DIMS`
and `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_MODEL_CACHE_DIR` (model-runtime.ts), and
`AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_HEAVY_MODE` (heavy-mode.ts). Env vars are inherently
machine/session-local -- there was no way for a team to commit a shared
default (e.g. "this monorepo always wants `embed_dims: 256`") without
every contributor separately exporting the same env var themselves.

The user asked for a project-level config file, explicitly requesting:
"a full config file loader which read a ai-context.config.yaml... env
vars become overrides on top of the file" -- i.e. env var still wins if
set, but the file becomes the new middle tier between env var and
built-in default.

## Decision

- One YAML file per project: `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml`, resolved
  via `resolveConfigFilePath(worktree)`. Placed inside `.opencode/`
  alongside this plugin's other worktree-local, team-shareable metadata
  (the repo-local backup, see ADR-0007; since ADR-0030 the cross-repo
  allow-list is a key of this file) -- NOT alongside the live SQLite store,
  which ADR-0003 deliberately keeps OUTSIDE the worktree.
- Precedence, applied per-setting rather than centrally: explicit
  function option (only relevant to this plugin's own tests) > env var
  (if explicitly set) > this config file > built-in default. Each
  consuming module (`resolveDataDir`, `resolveModelCacheDir`,
  `resolveOutputDims`, `isHeavyModeEnabled`) takes the config-file value
  as an additional, final-fallback parameter rather than the config file
  being centrally merged into `process.env` or similar -- keeps each
  setting's precedence contract visible and independently unit-testable
  at its own module, matching this codebase's existing per-module
  resolve-function style.
- YAML keys are snake_case (`data_dir`, `model_cache_dir`, `embed_dims`,
  `heavy_mode`) to match the file's own idiom, mapped to camelCase
  `AiContextConfigFile` fields for the TS side.
- Scope is exactly these 4 existing settings -- no new, previously
  un-configurable internals (e.g. the chunker's `maxLines`) were promoted
  to configurable as part of this change, to keep the increment bounded.
- Fault tolerance mirrors `backup.ts`'s per-row validation: a missing
  file, an empty file, malformed YAML, a non-mapping top level, or a
  wrong-typed known key are all `console.error`-logged and degrade to
  "no override from this key/file" -- never thrown. One bad line in a
  committed config file must not break the whole plugin for every
  contributor who pulls it.

## Consequences

- A team can now commit `embed_dims: 256` (say, for a very large
  monorepo) once, and every contributor gets it automatically, while
  still being able to locally override via an env var for one-off
  debugging without editing the committed file.
- `heavy-mode.ts`'s doc comment previously argued heavy mode is "not a
  repo config file setting... a machine/session performance trade-off,
  not a team convention to version-control" -- this is explicitly
  superseded: it's now also settable via the config file (a team CAN
  commit a shared default), with the env var still available as a
  per-machine override on top, matching the other 3 settings' identical
  treatment. Keeping heavy mode's precedence inconsistent with the other
  3 settings would have been a confusing, unjustified special case.
- `resolveOutputDims`'s existing "env var set but invalid falls straight
  to `undefined`" behavior was deliberately widened to "falls through to
  the config-file value instead" -- a backward-compatible expansion,
  since existing callers that never pass a config-file value see
  identical behavior to before.
- Adds `yaml` as a direct dependency (was already present transitively
  via `@opencode-ai/plugin` -> `effect`; pinned directly for stability/
  clarity rather than relying on the transitive resolution holding).

## Alternatives considered

- **JSON instead of YAML.** Rejected: no comments support, and this file
  is exactly the kind of "explain what each knob does, right next to
  it" document that benefits from inline comments (see the generated
  `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml`).
- **A single central "load all config" function that mutates
  `process.env` or a shared config object.** Rejected: would hide each
  setting's precedence contract behind one large function instead of
  keeping it visible (and independently unit-testable) at each
  consuming module, breaking from this codebase's existing
  `resolveDataDir`/`resolveModelCacheDir`/`resolveOutputDims` per-module
  pattern.
- **Config file overrides win over env vars.** Rejected per the user's
  explicit direction ("env vars become overrides on top of the file") --
  env vars stay the higher-precedence, machine-local escape hatch.

# ADR-0015: Single bundled plugin file, installed to OpenCode's global plugin directory

## Status

Accepted (packaging/setup, user-directed, 2026-09-16).

## Context

OpenCode loads **local plugins** directly from a plugin directory --
either `.opencode/plugins/` (project-level) or
`~/.config/opencode/plugins/` (global) -- with no build/install step of
its own: whatever JS/TS file is in that directory is loaded as-is at
startup. This package, however, is developed as a normal multi-module
TypeScript project (`src/hook/`, `src/storage/`, `src/embedding/`, etc.)
with `node_modules` dependencies, some of which ship native addons
(`better-sqlite3`, `onnxruntime-node`, `tokenizers`).

Two related questions needed answers: (1) how does a multi-file TS
source tree become the single file layout OpenCode's local-plugin
loader expects, and (2) where do a local plugin's native npm
dependencies get resolved from, since OpenCode does not run `npm
install`/`bun install` against the plugin directory itself.

Per OpenCode's own docs (https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins/#dependencies):
local plugins needing external packages must have a `package.json`
placed in OpenCode's own **config directory** (`~/.config/opencode/`),
against which OpenCode runs `bun install` at startup, caching the result
in `~/.cache/opencode/node_modules/`.

## Decision

- **Bundle, don't ship source.** `scripts/build.mjs` (esbuild) bundles
  `src/index.ts` into one file, `dist/accso-ai-context.js` (ESM,
  `node18` target, with a sourcemap). This plugin's OWN `src/` modules
  are inlined; native/non-inlinable runtime dependencies
  (`better-sqlite3`, `onnxruntime-node`, `tokenizers`,
  `@huggingface/hub`, `ignore`, `@opentelemetry/api`) are marked
  `external` and stay as plain `import` statements resolved from
  `node_modules` at runtime, same as any normal npm consumer would
  resolve them. `yaml` is deliberately NOT external -- it's pure JS with
  no native addon, so esbuild inlines it like this plugin's own code.
- **Install to the GLOBAL plugin directory** (`~/.config/opencode/
  plugins/accso-ai-context.js`), not the project-level one. This plugin
  is meant to be usable across every repo a contributor works in (see
  ADR-0002's per-project SQLite isolation, which already makes one
  globally-installed plugin instance safe to reuse across many
  worktrees/sessions) -- a project-level install would mean
  re-installing into every single repo instead of once per machine.
- **`scripts/install-plugin.sh`** copies the bundle to the global plugin
  directory, then merges (not overwrites) this plugin's runtime
  dependency versions into `~/.config/opencode/package.json`, so a
  second, unrelated plugin's own dependencies already listed there (or
  added later by that plugin's own setup script) are preserved rather
  than clobbered. OpenCode's own `bun install` at its next startup then
  resolves them -- this script does not run `bun`/`npm install` itself.
- **`accso-ai-context` as the file/tool-family name** (user-directed) --
  distinct from the working directory's own name
  (`ai-context-opencode-plugin`), matching what will be a different,
  more product-facing name once extracted to its own repository.
- **`mise.toml` + `mise run setup`** wraps `install-plugin.sh` (via a
  `depends: [build]` task chain) as the one-command entry point, and
  separately pins the dev/build/test Node toolchain version -- see the
  file's own header comment for why it's fully self-contained and
  doesn't merge with (or depend on) the parent `ai-context` monorepo's
  own `mise.toml`.

## Consequences

- A contributor (or, eventually, an end user once this is a published
  package) runs one command (`mise run setup`, or `npm run build &&
  ./scripts/install-plugin.sh` without mise) and gets a working global
  install, without needing to understand OpenCode's local-plugin
  dependency-resolution mechanism themselves.
- Re-running the install script after a rebuild is safe and idempotent:
  it always overwrites `accso-ai-context.js` itself (that's the point of
  reinstalling a new build) but only adds/updates this plugin's OWN
  dependency entries in the shared config-directory `package.json`,
  never removing or overwriting unrelated entries another plugin may
  have added.
- `scripts/build.mjs`'s `EXTERNAL_RUNTIME_DEPS` list and
  `install-plugin.sh`'s own copy of that list must be kept in sync
  manually (both files carry a comment saying so) -- a genuine, accepted
  maintenance cost of not sharing a single source of truth between an
  esbuild config and a bash script; revisit if this drifts in practice.
- Sourcemap (`accso-ai-context.js.map`) is copied alongside the bundle
  for stack traces during local debugging; `dist/` itself is
  gitignored -- it's a build artifact, not source.

## Alternatives considered

- **Publish to npm, use OpenCode's `plugin: [...]` config-file
  mechanism instead of a local file.** Rejected for now: this package
  isn't published yet (still living inside the parent monorepo, per
  this repo's own README) -- worth revisiting once it's extracted and
  versioned independently; nothing about the bundling step itself needs
  to change if that happens later.
- **Project-level install (`.opencode/plugins/`).** Rejected: would
  require every repo a contributor works in to separately receive the
  bundle/config, instead of once per machine -- see the isolation
  argument above for why one global install is already safe.
- **Ship `src/` unbundled and rely on OpenCode/Bun resolving relative
  imports directly.** Rejected: OpenCode's local-plugin loader expects
  a single loadable file per plugin, not a package directory with its
  own `node_modules`/multi-file module graph.

# ADR-0016: Current upstream grammar packages + `web-tree-sitter` 0.27 instead of `tree-sitter-wasms`

## Status

Accepted (2026-10). Refines ADR-0013 (WASM over native bindings stays).

## Context

`tree-sitter-wasms` 0.1.13 bundles grammars built with tree-sitter CLI
0.20 from old grammar versions (C# 0.20, Java 0.20, Kotlin 0.3,
Python 0.21, TypeScript/JavaScript 0.20) and pinned `web-tree-sitter` to
0.20.8. Modern syntax (C# 12+, Java 21, Python 3.12, TS 5.x, Kotlin 2.x)
produced ERROR nodes -- unacceptable for the symbol/import/call-graph
extraction that blast-radius analysis needs.

## Decision

- Depend on `web-tree-sitter` ^0.27 and the upstream grammar packages
  (`tree-sitter-c-sharp`, `-java`, `-python`, `-typescript` (also TSX),
  `-javascript`, `@tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-kotlin`), each of
  which ships a prebuilt `.wasm`. No grammar is built from source.
- Also load `tree-sitter-go`, `-rust`, `-ruby`, `-c` and `-cpp` the same
  way, so the symbol/import/call graph can cover those languages too.
  They are parser-loader entries only; chunking for them stays on the
  regex tier until graph extraction needs more.
- `parser-loader.ts` maps grammar names to `<package>/<file>.wasm` and
  resolves them with `createRequire`; `web-tree-sitter` is an esbuild
  external (it loads its own runtime `.wasm` from `node_modules`).
- `test/unit/grammar-modern-syntax.test.ts` guards each language with
  current-version syntax and asserts no ERROR nodes.

## Consequences

- Grammars track their languages; the unused `tree-sitter-wasms` grammars
  PHP and Swift are gone from the loader (Go, Rust, Ruby, C and C++
  are back via their upstream packages). Adding a
  language now means adding its upstream package + one map entry.
- Grammar packages must be installed next to the bundle (same as the
  other externals; see `scripts/install-plugin.sh`).
- Grammar ABI must stay compatible with the runtime (currently 14/15,
  supported by 0.27).

# ADR-0017: Use `bun:sqlite` inside OpenCode, `better-sqlite3` only under Node

## Status

Accepted (2026-10).

## Context

ADR-0002 chose `better-sqlite3` as the embedded store. OpenCode runs on
Bun, and Bun only runs a package's install script when the package is in
`trustedDependencies`. `better-sqlite3` was not, so its native addon was
never built, and Bun 1.3.14 does not throw when asked to load a missing
addon: it panics (`NAPI FATAL ERROR`, exit code 133) and takes the whole
OpenCode/ACP process down at plugin start.

## Decision

All three stores open their database through `src/storage/sqlite.ts`, a
thin adapter over the few calls they use (`exec`, `prepare`
`run/get/all`, `pragma`, `transaction`, `close`). Under Bun it uses the
built-in `bun:sqlite` (nothing to install or build); under Node (unit
tests, tooling) it uses `better-sqlite3`, required lazily so Bun never
tries to load it. `install-plugin.sh` no longer installs `better-sqlite3`.

## Consequences

- No native addon to build for storage; plugin start no longer depends on
  install scripts or prebuilt binaries.
- Two SQLite implementations behind one adapter: a behavior difference
  between them would only show up in one runtime (the adapter normalises
  the known one, `get()` returning `null` vs `undefined`).
- `onnxruntime-node` and `tokenizers` are still native addons; they are
  only loaded when the embedder is first used.

## Alternatives considered

- **Add `better-sqlite3` to `trustedDependencies`.** Rejected: needs a
  compiler or a network prebuild download on every machine, and a failed
  build still ends in a process crash rather than an error.
- **`bun:sqlite` only.** Rejected: the unit tests and tooling run on Node.

# ADR-0018: Report indexing progress via a status file and tool responses

## Status

Accepted (2026-10).

## Context

The first index of a repository embeds every file and runs for minutes.
Under JetBrains AI Assistant (ACP) the user saw nothing but CPU, RAM and
fan noise: the indexer reported no progress, and the channels that could
carry it are dead ends over ACP (`docs/observability.md`: TUI toasts and
injected chat messages never reach the client; `client.app.log` only lands
in opencode's log file). A failing file also aborted the whole batch, so
one unreadable file silently left the rest of a batch unindexed.

## Decision

- An in-memory progress tracker (`src/indexing/index-progress.ts`) is the
  single source of truth: phase, done/total, rate/ETA, and the files whose
  indexing failed.
- It is mirrored to `.opencode/ai-context/index-status.json`
  (`src/indexing/status-file.ts`): atomic write (tmp file + rename),
  throttled to one write per 2 s, except phase changes and newly failed
  files, which are written immediately. The file stays after the run
  (`phase: "done"`) so the last result remains inspectable.
- `index_status` returns the same data in an `indexing` block,
  including the status file path.
- `semantic_search`, `search_docs` and `analyze_impact` attach
  an `indexingNotice` while a run is active, so the agent tells the user
  that a missing hit may only mean "not indexed yet". Array results are
  wrapped as `{ indexingNotice, results }` only in that case.
- A file that fails to index is skipped and recorded (error, attempt
  count). The next watcher event for it, or the next startup pass, retries
  it; a success removes the entry, another failure increments `attempts`.
- `.opencode/ai-context/` is never indexed (`file-filter.ts`), otherwise
  every status write would come back as `file.watcher.updated`.

## Consequences

- Users can follow indexing with `while true; do clear; cat .opencode/ai-context/index-status.json; sleep 1; done`
  from any frontend, and the agent can relay progress in chat.
- The status file lives in the worktree and changes constantly. Add
  `.opencode/ai-context/index-status.json` to the project's `.gitignore`
  (the backup in the same directory is meant to be committed, this file
  is not). The plugin cannot enforce that.
- Two plugin instances (opencode bootstraps plugins twice) write the same
  file; the last write wins, which is harmless for a progress mirror.
- Failures are only held in memory for the current process; a restart
  re-attempts every file anyway.
- `semantic_search` output changes shape (array -> object) while indexing.

## Alternatives considered

- **TUI toasts / injected chat messages / `permission.ask`.** Rejected:
  confirmed not to reach ACP clients.
- **OS notifications for progress.** Rejected for per-step progress (too
  noisy); still an option for start/finish.
- **Status file under `data_dir` (outside the worktree).** Rejected: the
  user wants an easily accessible file, and excluding the directory in the
  filter removes the feedback-loop risk.
- **Aborting the batch on error (previous behavior).** Rejected: one bad
  file must not hide the rest of the repository from search.

# ADR-0019: Bounded memory during indexing

Status: accepted

## Context

Indexing a repository drove the opencode host process to 16-31 GB RSS and
filled the swap. Measured cause: onnxruntime memory grows quadratically with
the token count of one input (512 tokens ~0.5 GB, 4096 ~4.5 GB), while the
chunker bounded only lines, so a single 15 000-character chunk was enough.
Contributing: two plugin bootstraps per session indexed in parallel, the ORT
arena kept the peak, and `search()` loaded every vector per query.

## Decision

- Embedder caps tokens (`embed_max_tokens`, default 512); chunks are split to
  fit (`chunk-splitter.ts`); files over `max_file_bytes` are skipped.
- ORT session: no CPU arena/mem pattern, sequential execution, `embed_threads`.
- One shared runtime per worktree (`runtime-registry.ts`): one tracker, one
  model session, one startup pass, serial batches.
- Soft guard (`memory-guard.ts`, `max_memory_mb`, default 4096): GC + wait,
  then abort the run as `failed` with a readable reason.
- `search()` reads the table in rowid pages and keeps only the top-K.
- Native OS notifications for start/finish/failure (`os_notifications`).

## Consequences

- A hard RSS cap is impossible inside a Bun process; the guard is best effort,
  the token cap is the actual bound.
- Very long chunks are split, so retrieval granularity changes slightly.
- Skipped files are visible in `index-status.json` and retried on change.

# ADR-0020: Steer the agent to the context tools

Status: accepted

## Context

The agent preferred opencode's built-in grep/glob/read over this plugin's
tools. The `semantic_search` description even said "Prefer grep/glob first".
Skills are loaded on demand only, so they are the weakest lever.

## Decision

- Rewrite tool descriptions: `semantic_search` is used first for concept
  questions; grep/glob only for exact identifiers.
- Append a short rule block to the system prompt via the
  `experimental.chat.system.transform` hook (runs server-side, also under
  ACP). Config `agent_hint: false` disables it.
- New tool `repo_structure`: directory tree from the index (dirs first with
  file count and languages), `dir_path`, `depth`, and `project` to inspect
  another allowed project (cross-repo allowlist). Structure only, no
  summaries, so no extra model or RAM.
- `ai_context_telemetry_report` gets `view: "adoption"`: share of context-tool calls
  vs grep/glob, overall and per session, to measure whether steering works.
- No separate `list_recent_changes` tool: `index_status` already
  returns the most recently indexed files.

## Consequences

- The hook is marked experimental in opencode; if inactive, only the
  descriptions apply.
- The hint costs a few hundred tokens per request.
- Cross-project reads open the other project's SQLite store; `repo_structure`
  reads only file paths, not vectors.

## Alternatives considered

- Skill only: loaded on demand, rarely triggered.
- Nudge appended to broad grep results (`tool.execute.after`): deferred until
  the adoption numbers show it is needed.

## Amendment: admin tools

The hint and the descriptions of the admin tools now also carry the phrases a
user says: "create an ai context backup" maps to `ai_context_export_backup`,
"which files are indexed" to `ai_context_export_index_tree`, and the
descriptions of the project list, telemetry report and delete tools name their
trigger. `ai_context_delete_project` tells the agent to confirm with the user
first. Without these lines the agent never matched such requests to a tool.

# ADR-0021: Shared embedding worker outside opencode

Status: accepted

## Context

Every opencode instance (and every ACP session) loaded its own ONNX model
inside the host process. The model session, its memory arena and quadratic
attention peaks made the host grow to GBs, and a memory kill (exit 137)
took the whole opencode down. Several instances also duplicated the model.

## Decision

- The embedding model runs in ONE background process per user, started on
  demand by the first plugin instance and shared by all others.
- Transport: newline-delimited JSON over a unix socket
  (`<data dir>/embed-worker.sock`, or `$TMPDIR` if the path would exceed the
  socket path limit). The worker is the arbiter: a second worker finding a
  live socket exits, a stale socket file is replaced.
- The worker script `ai-context-worker.mjs` is installed next to (not in)
  `~/.config/opencode/plugins/`, since opencode loads every file there as a
  plugin. It resolves native deps from `~/.config/opencode/node_modules`.
- It is started with the host binary and `BUN_BE_BUN=1` (opencode is a
  compiled Bun; the variable makes it run a script like `bun`; verified with
  opencode 1.18.34). Plain node/bun ignore the variable.
- Lifecycle: exits after 10 min without clients, or after a request once its
  RSS exceeds `max_memory_mb`; clients then reconnect and respawn (one retry).
  Inference runs one request at a time across all clients.
- If the worker cannot start, the client falls back to in-process embedding
  (with a problem report). `shared_worker: false` or
  `AI_CONTEXT_SHARED_WORKER=0` disables it.
- Log: `<data dir>/embed-worker.log`.

## Consequences

- The host stays small; a runaway model only costs the worker.
- The first instance's embedding settings (threads, max tokens, model cache,
  dims) win for the worker's lifetime.
- Needs `ai-context-worker.mjs` installed (`scripts/install-plugin.sh`);
  without it the plugin embeds in-process as before.
- A detached process must exit reliably; idle exit and SIGTERM cleanup cover
  this.

## Alternatives considered

- Moving indexing (not only embedding) into the worker: larger change, the
  SQLite writes are cheap; may follow.
- Requiring `node`/`bun` on PATH: not guaranteed for ACP users.

# ADR-0022: Move the indexer into the shared worker

Status: proposed (plan only, not implemented)

## Context

ADR-0021 moved the embedding model out of opencode. The rest of indexing
still runs inside every opencode instance: directory walk, file reads,
Tree-sitter WASM parsing, chunking, graph extraction and the SQLite writes.
That costs CPU and memory per instance and needs a per-process guard
(`runtime-registry.ts`) so the two bootstraps of one session do not index
in parallel. Two instances on the same worktree still run two indexers.

## Decision (proposed)

The worker also indexes. The plugin sends `index { worktree, paths | "all" }`
and gets progress events back; the worker owns Tree-sitter parsers, chunker,
graph extraction and the writes to the project's SQLite files.

- One indexing queue per worktree in the worker, so concurrent instances
  never index the same project twice and never hit `database is locked`.
- Progress events feed the existing tracker and `index-status.json`
  (ADR-0018); the plugin keeps the status file and OS notifications.
- Memory guard and `max_memory_mb` apply to the worker; opencode stays small.
- Search, tools and hooks stay in the plugin (read-only on the stores,
  WAL allows readers during writes).
- The worker needs config per request (exclude patterns, `max_file_bytes`,
  chunk limits), sent with each `index` call rather than fixed at spawn.
- Fallback stays: if the worker is unreachable, index in-process as today.

## Phases

1. Protocol: `index`/`progress`/`done`/`failed` messages, worker-side queue
   per worktree (tests with a fake indexer, like `worker.test.ts`).
2. Move `createIndexer` + walker + graph indexer behind an interface the
   worker implements; plugin calls it through the client.
3. Wire progress into the tracker; keep in-process fallback.
4. Measure RSS and CPU per instance before and after.

## Consequences

- Lower per-instance memory and a single indexer per project.
- The worker becomes a larger piece to keep stable; a crash interrupts
  indexing (the existing delta reconciliation resumes it).
- Bundling Tree-sitter WASM and grammars into the worker bundle must be
  checked (they are external packages resolved from the config dir).

## Alternatives considered

- Keep indexing in-process and only bound it further: simpler, but each
  instance still pays the parser and file-content memory.
- One worker per project: more processes, no gain over one queue per project.

# ADR-0023: Tool naming scheme and description rules

Status: accepted

## Context

Tool names mixed two styles by build order, not by role: `search_docs` and
`index_status` carried the `ai_context_` prefix although agents use them for
research, while `telemetry_report` (admin) had none. `semantic_search` also
claimed to cover "code and docs", but Markdown docs are tree-indexed and not
searchable through it, so agents searched docs with the wrong tool.

## Decision

- **Research tools** (used by the agent while working), no prefix:
  `semantic_search`, `repo_structure`, `analyze_impact`, `search_docs`,
  `index_status`.
- **Admin tools**, prefix `ai_context_`: `ai_context_list_projects`,
  `ai_context_delete_project`, `ai_context_export_backup`,
  `ai_context_allow_repo`, `ai_context_telemetry_report`.
- A test enforces the scheme.
- Descriptions state: what it covers and what it does NOT (code vs docs),
  when to use it, what it returns, and the next step (`read` with the line
  range). `index_status` states its trigger: empty or partial results, or an
  `indexingNotice`.

## Consequences

- Renamed: `ai_context_search_docs` -> `search_docs`,
  `ai_context_index_status` -> `index_status`,
  `telemetry_report` -> `ai_context_telemetry_report`. No aliases are kept.
  Prompts or skills that use the old names must be updated.
- Unprefixed names could collide with future built-in opencode tools; the
  five names are specific enough to accept that risk.

# ADR-0024: Retrieval quality roadmap (no vector DB, symbol lookup, deterministic summaries)

## Status

Accepted (2026-10-06). Implemented: FTS5 BM25 + RRF, cross-encoder reranker,
path/symbol embed prefix, `find_symbol`, file summaries (deterministic, optional
OpenAI-compatible LLM) and best-effort enabling of the native `lsp` tool
(`OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL`, only effective if the host reads flags after
plugin load). Not done: baseline benchmark, ANN index.

## Context

Open questions: is a vector DB needed for better search, and how do we cover
the original stack's L1 summaries, routing and `resolve_symbol` without Docker?

- Brute-force cosine is exact; an ANN index only makes search faster, not
  better (and slightly lossy). Measured: ~110 ms at 2k, ~580 ms at 10k,
  ~1.75 s at 30k chunks.
- Routing: the original stack already removed its routing LLM; the calling
  agent drives retrieval.
- L1 summaries in the original come from an LLM server (LM Studio).
- `resolve_symbol` in the original is LSP definition/references/hover, which
  opencode's native `lsp` tool provides.

## Decision (plan, in order)

1. **Baseline benchmark** on two indexed projects (fixed query set, recall@k),
   before changing ranking.
2. **FTS5 BM25 + reciprocal rank fusion** replacing the keyword boost; then a
   small ONNX **cross-encoder reranker** in the shared worker.
3. **Embed context**: prefix chunk text with path and symbol name.
4. **`find_symbol` tool** on the existing symbol index (name/prefix to file,
   line, kind, signature); keep the native `lsp` tool for compiler-grade
   answers and mention it in the agent hint. Verify the `lsp` tool is enabled
   in the installed opencode version first.
5. **Deterministic file summaries** from AST/graph (exports, signatures, doc
   comments, imports), embedded as a file-level vector. An LLM-generated
   variant stays optional and opt-in.
6. **ANN index** (e.g. hnswlib/usearch, inside the worker) only above roughly
   20-30k chunks per project; before that, `embed_dims` truncation and a
   vector cache in the worker.

Each step is test-first and gated by the benchmark from step 1.

## Consequences

- No vector database, no Docker, no LLM server required.
- No ported `resolve_symbol`; the lookup tool is lighter and the `lsp` tool
  covers the rest.
- Quality gains are measured, not assumed.

# ADR-0025: Resumable indexing and cross-process index lease

## Status

Accepted (2026-10-06).

## Context

Every ACP session is its own opencode process. Each ran the startup pass and
re-embedded **every** file (no change detection), all writing to the same
SQLite files: duplicated CPU/RAM, lock contention, and no way to continue where
a previous run stopped. The in-process guard (ADR-0021 runtime registry) does
not span processes.

## Decision

1. **Fingerprints:** after a file is fully indexed, the vector store records
   `size:mtime` (`file_state` table). Files whose fingerprint matches (and that
   have chunks) are skipped, so a restart, a second session or an interrupted
   run continues with the remaining files. Failed files have no fingerprint and
   are retried. A changed `EMBED_FORMAT_VERSION` clears fingerprints with the chunks.
2. **Stale files:** the startup pass removes indexed files that are gone from the
   walk (deleted or newly excluded).
3. **Lease:** `index.lock` next to the project database (`pid` + heartbeat every
   10 s). Indexing batches run while holding it; another process waits (polls
   every 3 s) and then only finds the unfinished files. A lease of a dead
   process or without heartbeat for 45 s is taken over.

## Consequences

- One indexing process per project at a time; later sessions are fast.
- A waiting process shows phase `scanning` and may overwrite
  `index-status.json` until it gets the lease.
- Restored backups carry no fingerprints, so the first pass re-indexes once.
- Processes running an older plugin version do not honour the lease.

# ADR-0026: Cross-repo tools and parallel indexing

## Status

Accepted (2026-10-06). Amended by [ADR-0030](0030-allowlist-in-config-yaml.md): the allowlist is stored in the config YAML (still read live).

## Context

1. Only `semantic_search` and `repo_structure` could look into other allowed
   projects; `find_symbol`, `analyze_impact` and `search_docs` were limited to
   the current repo, and a repo added with `ai_context_allow_repo` took effect
   only after a restart (the allowlist was read once at startup).
2. Indexing was slow: the shared worker ran one inference at a time, the
   indexer handled one file at a time, and the file-summary LLM call blocked
   the embedding of the same file.

## Decision

1. **Cross-repo:** all research tools accept an optional `project` key (from
   `ai_context_list_projects`). `find_symbol` and `analyze_impact` use the
   other project's `graph.sqlite`, `search_docs` its `doc-trees.sqlite`. Unknown
   or not allowed keys return an error listing the allowed ones. A graph/doc
   file that does not exist is never created in the other project's folder.
   `ai_context_allow_repo` opens the stores immediately.
2. **Skill:** the bundled `cross-repo` skill describes the sequence
   `ai_context_list_projects` → `ai_context_allow_repo` → tool with `project`.
3. **Parallel indexing:** `embed_concurrency` (default 3) sets both the number
   of files indexed in parallel (`fileConcurrency`) and the inference slots of
   the worker (`concurrency`, default 1 when unset). The summary LLM request is
   started before the file's chunks are embedded and awaited afterwards.
   Defaults raised to `embed_threads: 6`, `max_memory_mb: 6144`.

## Consequences

- Faster indexing at the cost of CPU and transient RAM; `embed_concurrency: 1`
  restores sequential behaviour.
- Paths in cross-repo results are relative to the other repo; `read` only works
  inside the current project.
- The same file appearing twice in one batch could be indexed concurrently;
  startup batches contain each file once, so this is accepted.
- Not measured yet: real speed-up on a fresh index (see `docs/status.md`).

# ADR-0027: Self-healing re-index on startup

## Status

Accepted (2026-10-08).

## Context

The startup pass skips a file whose `size:mtime` fingerprint is unchanged. That
made changes to *how* files are indexed invisible: documents chunked by an
older version stayed chunks, doc trees without summaries (LLM offline) stayed
empty, and tree-indexed documents were re-read on every start because the skip
test required code chunks. Trees of deleted documents were never removed,
since the stale-file scan only looked at chunks.

## Decision

- The stored fingerprint carries a representation suffix: `#doc<DOC_INDEX_VERSION>`
  for tree-indexed document types; for code `#code<N>` only when
  `CODE_INDEX_VERSION > 1`, and `#nosum` while file summaries are off. Switching
  summaries on, or bumping a version, re-indexes only the affected file kind;
  stores written before this ADR stay valid for code. `EMBED_FORMAT_VERSION`
  remains the full-store reset.
- An unchanged file is skipped only if its index is healthy: code needs chunks;
  a document needs a tree and no chunks (documents are trees only), and a tree
  without any summary is rebuilt while a summarizer is configured (cheap: no
  embedding; the LLM is skipped after three failures).
- The stale-file scan includes doc-tree paths (`DocTreeStore.listPaths`).
- Fallback summaries (amendment, 2026-10-12): when `summary_llm` is configured
  but a code file's summary had to be the deterministic text, the fingerprint
  gets a `detsum` flag (`<fp>#detsum`, or `+detsum` after other suffixes). On a
  later start with an LLM configured, a flagged file gets only its summary chunk
  rewritten (reason `summaries`, no re-embedding of the other chunks); the flag
  is dropped when the LLM answered, kept otherwise. Without a configured LLM the
  flag is ignored.
- Forced re-index (amendment, 2026-10-12): the config keys `reindex_chunks` and
  `reindex_summaries` make the next startup pass ignore fingerprints (reason
  `upgrade`). Chunks only: files are re-chunked and re-embedded, the stored
  summary chunk is kept. Summaries only: just the summary chunk is rewritten
  (documents are rebuilt as a whole, their summaries live in the tree). Both:
  full re-index. After a run without failed files or abort the plugin sets the
  flags back to `false` by editing only those lines of the config file; an
  incomplete run keeps them on so it is repeated.

- Visibility: the indexer classifies every file before the run
  (`new`, `changed`, `removed`, `upgrade` = new index format, `repair`,
  `summaries`) and reports only files that need work. Up-to-date files are
  not counted, so a normal start no longer announces "Indexing started: N
  files". `index-status.json` carries `reasons` (counts per reason). Healing
  (`upgrade`/`repair`/`summaries`) pops up even for a few files: "Updating
  index: 42 files (40 new index format, 2 repaired)" and "Index update
  finished"; plain new/changed runs keep the old popups and the 20-file
  threshold.

## Consequences

- A flagged file is retried on every start while the LLM stays down (one cheap
  attempt, no re-embedding).
- Upgrading re-indexes documents once; code files are untouched.
- When the summary server is permanently down, documents are re-parsed on each
  start (three quick failed calls, then none).
- Changing the chunker or doc-tree builder now requires bumping the matching
  version constant in `src/indexing/indexing.ts`.

# ADR-0028: Compact, sharded backup (float16 vectors, hash shards)

## Status

Accepted (2026-10-08). Amends [ADR-0007](0007-repo-local-versionable-backup.md).

## Context

The chunk backup was one `index.jsonl` with vectors as JSON float arrays: 63 MB
for 3,711 chunks (17 KB per vector), close to GitHub's 100 MB push limit and
growing with the repo. Git cannot delta-compress float noise, so every changed
copy also bloated history.

## Decision

- Vectors are stored as base64 float16 (`vector16`, 2 bytes per dimension,
  about 2 KB instead of 17 KB). Precision loss is below 1e-3 relative; export
  after import is byte-stable because the values are already half precision.
- Rows go to `index-NNNN.jsonl` shards chosen by a stable FNV-1a hash of the
  file path, `maxShardBytes` (default 10 MiB) bounds the target size. The shard
  count is a power of two estimated from chunk count and average row size, so
  it changes rarely, a file's chunks stay together and a change rewrites one
  shard. Rows stay sorted by id inside a shard.
- Export deletes the legacy `index.jsonl` and stale shards first. Import reads
  the legacy file (float arrays) and all shards; per-row validation and
  skipping of broken rows is unchanged. Doc-tree and graph backups are small
  and unchanged.

## Consequences

- The measured backup shrinks from 63 MB to 10.8 MB (two shards).
- Old committed backups stay importable; the next export migrates them.
- Restored vectors differ from the originals by half-precision rounding; with
  brute-force cosine search this is negligible, but a benchmark would confirm.
- Beyond roughly 50k chunks a further 2x is possible with int8 vectors behind
  a new row key; not needed yet.

# ADR-0029: Opt-in per repository (`enabled`) and a config file generated with defaults

## Status

Accepted (2026-10-12). Amends [ADR-0014](0014-project-config-file-precedence.md).

## Context

The plugin started indexing every repository opencode was opened in, including
ones where nobody wanted it (cost: CPU, RAM, a model download, files written into
`.opencode/`). The generated config file listed every key only as a comment, so
users still had to read the documentation to learn the effective settings.

## Decision

- New top-level key `enabled` in `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml`. It is
  **opt-in**: absent, `false` or unparsable (malformed file, wrong type) means
  off. `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_ENABLED` (`1`/`true`, `0`/`false`) overrides the file in
  both directions (precedence as in ADR-0014).
- Off means: the plugin returns no hooks. The config file is still created when
  missing, but nothing else happens: no index or doc-tree store, no startup or
  watcher indexing, no worker, no tools, no agent hint, no bundled skills, no
  `.opencode/.gitignore`, no popups. The gate sits right after the config is
  loaded in `createAiContextHooks`.
- The generated file starts with `enabled: false` and then lists every setting
  with its **actual built-in default** as an active value. Machine-specific
  (`data_dir`, `model_cache_dir`, `embed_dims`) and optional (`exclude`,
  `heavy_mode`) keys stay commented. `config-template.test.ts` asserts that the
  template parses to exactly the code's default constants, so the two cannot
  drift apart.
- Existing config files are never rewritten. A file without `enabled` therefore
  switches the plugin off after the upgrade (strict opt-in, chosen on purpose);
  this repository's own file got `enabled: true`.

- Secrets stay out of the committed file (amendment, 2026-10-12): `summary_llm`
  takes no literal `api_key` (ignored with a warning); the key is read from the
  environment variable named by `api_key_env` (default
  `AI_CONTEXT_SUMMARY_LLM_API_KEY`), and the built-in default key `omlx` is gone.
  On HTTP 401 the summarizer raises `SummaryLlmAuthError` ("API key not set" or
  "rejected", with the `export ...` command); the plugin shows it as an OS popup
  and as a `notices` entry in `index-status.json` / `index_status`, cleared when
  the next run starts. Summaries fall back to the deterministic text as before.

## Consequences

- Setups that relied on the default key `omlx` must export
  `AI_CONTEXT_SUMMARY_LLM_API_KEY=omlx` once.
- Breaking for existing users: add `enabled: true` once per repository (or set
  the environment variable).
- Defaults copied into a user's file no longer follow later changes of the
  built-in defaults; users who never edit a line keep the old value.
- `summary_llm` is active in the template, so after enabling, file content goes
  to the local default server (`127.0.0.1:8000`), exactly as before; `summary_llm:
  false` turns it off.
- Tests that exercise the plugin set `AI_CONTEXT_PLUGIN_ENABLED=1` at the top of
  the test file; disabled-behaviour tests unset it explicitly.

## Amendment: index tree and error log files

Two generated files join `index-status.json` in `.opencode/ai-context/`:
`index-tree.md` (tool `ai_context_export_index_tree`, refreshed after each
completed indexing run) lists the indexed files with export date, repository,
branch and commit; `error.log.md` collects every reported problem, failed file
and failed run, size-capped. Both are git-ignored and written only when the
plugin is enabled (entries recorded before the enabled gate are buffered and
dropped if the plugin stays off), so a disabled plugin still only creates the
config file.

## Alternatives considered

- Default-on with an `enabled: false` kill switch: keeps upgrades non-breaking
  but leaves the plugin running in repositories that never asked for it.
- Rewriting existing config files to add missing keys: would edit user files and
  discard their formatting.

# ADR-0030: Cross-repo allowlist lives in `ai-context.config.yaml`

## Status

Accepted (2026-10-19). Amends [ADR-0014](0014-project-config-file-precedence.md)
and [ADR-0026](0026-cross-repo-tools-and-parallel-indexing.md).

## Context

The allowlist of other indexed projects lived in a separate file,
`.opencode/ai-context/config/allowed-repos.json`, next to the generated
artifacts (status, backup). It is a human decision, not generated data, so it
was in the wrong place, and the project had two config locations and formats.
The file was separate because the tool writes it as JSON and the allowlist is
applied live, while the YAML is read once at startup.

## Decision

- The allowlist is the `allowed_repos` key (list of project names, no hash) of
  `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml`.
- `ai_context_allow_repo` edits the key in place with the `yaml` document API:
  comments and other keys stay. A short comment above the key says the plugin
  writes it. Malformed YAML makes the write fail with an error instead of
  overwriting the file.
- The key is re-read from disk on every call (not part of the startup config),
  so changes still apply without a restart (ADR-0026).
- Rule of thumb: `.opencode/ai-context.config.yaml` holds what people decide;
  `.opencode/ai-context/` holds what the plugin generates.
- Migration: the first read imports a legacy
  `ai-context/config/allowed-repos.json` into the YAML and removes it (and the
  empty `config/` folder).

## Consequences

- One config file, no `config/` subfolder.
- An allowlist change shows up in the same diff as other settings; review it
  like any config change ([data boundary](../data-boundary.md)).
- A concurrent manual edit of the YAML and a plugin write can collide; the
  window is small because the list rarely changes.

## Alternatives considered

- Keep the JSON file and only flatten its path: smallest change, but leaves two
  config formats.
- Move the whole config into `.opencode/ai-context/`: mixes hand-edited config
  with generated and ignored files.

# ADR-0031: OpenCode 2.x entry point, host-specific LSP handling, stronger grep/glob steering

## Status

Accepted (2026-10-28). Amends [ADR-0015](0015-single-bundled-plugin-file.md) and
[ADR-0020](0020-steer-agent-to-context-tools.md).

## Context

- OpenCode 2.x replaces the plugin API: a plugin is `Plugin.define({ id, setup(ctx) })` from
  `@opencode/plugin`; tools are JSON-Schema definitions registered with `ctx.tool.transform`,
  hooks are registered per domain (`ctx.tool.hook`, `ctx.session.hook`, `ctx.event.subscribe`).
  V1 plugin implementations do not run there. The `@opencode-ai/plugin` package (zod `tool()`
  helper) is not available at runtime.
- 2.x accepts the `lsp` config key but runs no language servers and has no LSP tool or API.
  The plugin used to switch 1.x's LSP on and told the agent to "confirm with `lsp`".
- Agents still explore with `glob **/*.kt` or descriptive greps although the system-prompt hint
  says otherwise.

## Decision

- **One bundle, two entries.** The default export is `{ id, setup, server }`: 2.x reads
  `setup`, 1.x (>= 1.18.29) reads `server`. The core (`createAiContextHooks`) stays
  host-neutral with a 1.x-shaped hook set (`AiContextHooks`); `hook/v2-plugin.ts` maps it onto
  the 2.x API (tools, `execute.before/after`, `context`, `compaction`, `filesystem.changed`,
  cleanup). No runtime import of any OpenCode package.
- **Own tool helper.** `tools/tool-def.ts` keeps the `tool({ description, args, execute })`
  shape with zod args (zod is bundled). 1.x gets the object as is; 2.x gets
  `z.toJSONSchema(args)` and validation/defaults inside `execute`.
- **LSP is host specific** (`host: "v1" | "v2"` dep of `createAiContextHooks`; the 1.x
  `server()` passes "v1", the 2.x `setup()` "v2", default "v2"). On "v1" nothing changes: the
  `config` hook enables LSP (never over `lsp: false`), and the agent hint, `find_symbol` and
  `analyze_impact` point to the native `lsp` tool. On "v2" the `config` hook is not used, nothing
  is switched on and no text mentions `lsp`; ambiguous edges are confirmed by reading the call
  site, exact-identifier grep, compiler/tests. A plugin-owned LSP bridge for both is planned
  ([lsp-roadmap](../lsp-roadmap.md)).
- **Steering.** In addition to the system-prompt rule: (1) suffix on the native `grep`/`glob`
  descriptions (`tool.definition` on 1.x, `ctx.tool.transform` + `editor.update` on 2.x);
  (2) a note appended to the result of exploratory grep/glob calls (`search-nudge.ts`):
  extension-only glob, multi-word/many-branch grep, empty result of an exact grep. Exact-token greps are not
  nudged. All follow `agent_hint`.
- `shell` joins `bash` as a file-changing tool for the rescan fallback.

## Consequences

- 2.x users get the tools, indexing, telemetry and steering; 1.x keeps working until dropped.
- The nudge text is part of tool results: small token cost, only on exploratory calls.
- Verified on 2.2.0: `filesystem.changed` is published only for files watched through the
  experimental `fs.watch` API, and the plugin context has no fs domain, so there is no
  project-wide watcher event. On 2.x the rescan after `shell`/`edit`/`write` calls is the
  indexing trigger (a probe `.ts` file was searchable via `find_symbol` within seconds); changes
  made outside the agent (IDE, `git pull`) are picked up by a throttled rescan on `session.idle`, the
  startup pass or `ai_context_rescan`. File-editing tools (`edit`/`write`/`apply_patch`) are indexed
  per file from their arguments instead of walking the repo; `shell` and IDE tools still rescan fully.
- **Tool visibility on 2.x.** A plugin tool without `options.codemode: false` is only reachable
  through Code Mode `execute`, and the Code Mode catalog is partial, so agents did not find the
  lookup tools. `toV2Tool` now sets `codemode: false` for `DIRECT_TOOLS` (`semantic_search`,
  `find_symbol`, `repo_structure`, `analyze_impact`, `search_docs`, `index_status`) and `true`
  for the `ai_context_*` admin tools, which keeps their schemas out of every request. On 2.x the
  agent hint (`CODE_MODE_HINT`) states which tools are direct and how to reach the rest. Details and
  a verification checklist: [opencode-v2-plugin-checklist.md](../opencode-v2-plugin-checklist.md).
- Run a real 2.x session after each release (tools listed, hooks fire, nudges visible).

## Alternatives considered

- Separate 2.x package: doubles releases for no gain while 1.x is still in use.
- Blocking grep/glob in `execute.before`: hostile to legitimate greps; rejected for now.

# Runtime Debugging (xdebug_*)

## Goal
Use debugger evidence to answer concrete runtime questions when static code reading is not enough or to confirm ideas or results made by static analysis, including whether execution reaches or does not reach agent-selected code locations via breakpoints or tracepoints.

## When To Use This Guidance
Use this guidance when at least one of the following is true:
- runtime state or control-flow evidence is needed (actual values, branch taken, call order, thread context, or whether execution reaches a chosen location), and it cannot be derived confidently from source/logs;
- finding the relevant path would otherwise require reading many files or tracing a long call chain manually;
- the user explicitly asks to use the debugger (breakpoints, stepping, inspect values, debugger session).

If the user manually activates or refers to debugging, treat that as an explicit request to launch and use the debugger when the required tools are available. Do not reduce a manual activation to a conceptual discussion about debugging.

If the user's codebase domain itself contains debug-related concepts, reason explicitly about whether the user is talking about their code or actually asking you to launch and use the debugger. Do not treat domain concepts, features, modes, log categories, flags, or identifiers named `debug` or `debugger` as a debugger request by default.

## Activation Gate (tool availability)
Use this guidance only when debugger MCP tools are available in the current session.

Minimum required set:
- `xdebug_set_breakpoint`
- `xdebug_start_debugger_session`
- `xdebug_control_session`
- `xdebug_get_stack`
- at least one value tool: `xdebug_get_frame_values` or `xdebug_get_value_by_path` or `xdebug_evaluate_expression`
- `get_run_configurations` (needed for entry point discovery and run config resolution)

If this minimum set is not available:
- state the blocker explicitly;
- do not force a debugger workflow;
- switch to the best fallback path (e.g. `references/explore.md`).

Tool names in this file reflect this session's live MCP tool schema — bare names with **no `idea_` prefix** (e.g. `xdebug_start_debugger_session`, not `idea_xdebug_start_debugger_session`), invoked via the `idea-mcp-execute_tool` dispatcher — confirmed live 2026-08-13. Always treat the live schema as the source of truth if it differs.

## Initial Triage Before Debugging
Start with minimal static triage (error text, stack trace, and nearby source). Start debugger work when one of these is true:
- static analysis leaves multiple plausible runtime hypotheses;
- deciding between hypotheses requires concrete runtime values or exact control flow;
- stepping through the code is cheaper than reading a large cross-file path;
- the user explicitly requested debugger actions.

Before starting a new debugger run, assess whether there is already a current relevant debugger session that can be reused.

When debugger work is chosen, set the first breakpoint early and collect concrete evidence before making runtime behavior changes.

## Mandatory Runtime Evidence
Before making code edits for runtime behavior issues when debugger evidence is available, collect this minimum evidence:
- paused location (file/line) from a suspended debug session;
- top call path via `xdebug_get_stack`;
- when control-flow reachability is part of the question, evidence that execution did or did not hit an explicitly chosen breakpoint or tracepoint;
- at least one concrete runtime value via `xdebug_get_frame_values`, `xdebug_get_value_by_path`, or `xdebug_evaluate_expression`.

Do not assert runtime conclusions before this evidence is captured unless you have already stated a clear blocker that makes debugger evidence unavailable or useless for this task.

## Reproduction Mode Selection
Choose the execution mode before starting:
1. `AUTO`: the agent can run and rerun the scenario directly (run config, test, command, endpoint). Use `xdebug_start_debugger_session` to launch with debugging, or `execute_run_configuration` for a non-debug run when you only need output or exit code.
2. `ASSISTED`: reproduction requires a user-only action (UI flow, auth, external dependency, hardware interaction).
3. `HYBRID`: try `AUTO` once or twice, then switch to `ASSISTED` if the failure does not reproduce.

Practical heuristic:
- if the candidate debug target is a test, default to `AUTO`;
- never ask the user to reproduce before breakpoints are prepared.

## Test Task Execution
- If the task is about tests, failing tests, flaky tests, or reproducing a bug through a test, use the narrowest test-running mechanism available in the current session.
- To debug a test: use `xdebug_start_debugger_session(filePath, line)` pointing at the test method or `xdebug_start_debugger_session(configurationName)` for an existing test run configuration. To run a test without debugging (e.g., to confirm it fails before setting breakpoints): use `execute_run_configuration` with the same targeting modes.
- After triggering the test scenario, inspect the resulting debugger state with `xdebug_get_debugger_status()` and continue the investigation in the relevant session.
- When the task is test-driven, do not ask the user to rerun the test manually unless no available test-running path can reproduce it or the reproduction requires user-only setup.

## Argument Hygiene
- Optional parameters are either omitted/null or intentionally set to a real value; omitted means omitted.
- Do not encode omitted optional parameters with placeholder strings such as `""`, `"/"`, `"__omit__"`, `"."`, fake paths, or other sentinels.
- Treat debugger IDs and paths as opaque runtime data: copy them from tool outputs instead of synthesizing them.

## Session Binding
- Before preparing new breakpoints or launching a new session, call `xdebug_get_debugger_status()`.
- If there is an active relevant session, continue inside it instead of starting another one.
- After `xdebug_get_debugger_status()` or `xdebug_start_debugger_session()`, capture the exact `sessionId` and reuse it in all session-scoped calls.
- If a session stops, times out, or disappears, do not reuse the old `sessionId`; refresh it with `xdebug_get_debugger_status()` before the next session-scoped call.

## Run Configuration Resolution
